biology.A1.biochemistry.notes:
# Biochemistry

> [!intro] Biomolecules and an overview of metabolic pathways — shared with chemistry.

## Molecules of life

Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids each have structures suiting their roles. This connects directly to chemistry's biomolecules topic.

## Metabolism

Metabolic pathways are linked reactions building (anabolism) or breaking down (catabolism) molecules, controlled by enzymes, releasing or storing energy.

```formula Key facts
Anabolism builds; catabolism breaks down
Enzymes control every metabolic step
Biomolecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Is building a protein from amino acids anabolic or catabolic?
> >
> > **Solution.** Anabolic — small monomers (amino acids) are joined into a larger molecule, which requires energy.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe major biomolecules
- Outline metabolism
- Relate structure to function

---

biology.A1.cell-biology-depth.notes:
# Cell Biology at Depth

> [!intro] Membrane transport, the cell cycle, and cell division (mitosis and meiosis).

## Cell cycle and division

Cells grow and divide in a controlled cycle. Mitosis makes two identical cells (growth, repair); meiosis makes four genetically varied gametes (reproduction).

## Why meiosis matters

Meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles genes, creating the variation that Genetics I described. It is the molecular source of inherited diversity.

```formula Key facts
Mitosis: 2 identical diploid cells (growth/repair)
Meiosis: 4 varied haploid gametes
Meiosis halves chromosome number and shuffles genes
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why must gametes be made by meiosis, not mitosis?
> >
> > **Solution.** Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the normal diploid number, and it creates genetic variation.

## What you should be able to do

- Detail membrane transport
- Describe the cell cycle
- Compare mitosis and meiosis

---

> [!intro] Detailed digestive, circulatory, excretory and nervous systems.

## Systems in detail

Each system is examined at organ and tissue level: the kidney filters blood and balances water; neurons transmit electrical impulses across synapses.

## Integration

Kidney: filter blood, then reabsorb needed substances

biology.A1.molecular-genetics.subject: biology
biology.A1.molecular-genetics.title: Molecular Genetics
biology.A1.molecular-genetics.summary: Transcription, translation and gene regulation in detail.
biology.A1.molecular-genetics.notes:
# Molecular Genetics

> [!intro] Transcription, translation and gene regulation in detail.

## Gene expression

Transcription copies a gene to mRNA; translation reads mRNA codons (three bases) to build a protein from amino acids. The genetic code maps codons to amino acids.

## Regulation

Cells switch genes on and off so the right proteins are made at the right time — why a nerve cell and a skin cell differ despite identical DNA.

```formula Key facts
Codon = 3 bases = 1 amino acid
Transcription (nucleus) then translation (ribosome)
Gene regulation → cell specialisation
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** How can a nerve cell and a skin cell have identical DNA yet differ?
> >
> > **Solution.** Gene regulation switches different genes on in each cell, so they make different proteins and take on different roles.

## What you should be able to do

- Detail transcription and translation
- Explain the genetic code
- Describe gene regulation

---

biology.A1.plant-physiology-depth.notes:
# Plant Physiology at Depth

> [!intro] Mechanisms of photosynthesis and respiration, transport and plant hormones.

## Photosynthesis mechanism

Photosynthesis has light-dependent reactions (capturing energy) and light-independent reactions (fixing carbon). Understanding both explains how plants store energy.

## Control and transport

Transpiration pulls water up; plant hormones (auxins) control growth toward light. Plants sense and respond to their environment.

```formula Key facts
Light reactions capture energy; Calvin cycle fixes carbon
Transpiration pulls water up the xylem
Auxins cause growth toward light (phototropism)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why does a plant on a windowsill bend toward the window?
> >
> > **Solution.** Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, elongating those cells more, so the shoot bends toward the light (phototropism).

## What you should be able to do

- Detail photosynthesis mechanisms
- Explain plant transport in depth
- Describe plant hormones

---

# Biotechnology

> [!intro] Recombinant DNA, PCR, applications and ethics — linked to argumentation.

## Engineering DNA

Recombinant DNA technology cuts and pastes genes between organisms; PCR amplifies tiny DNA samples. These tools power medicine, agriculture and forensics.

## Ethics

Powerful tools raise questions — GM crops, gene editing, privacy. Reasoning through them connects to the argumentation skills built in English.

```formula Key facts
PCR amplifies (copies) DNA
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites
Recombinant DNA joins genes from different sources
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why is PCR useful in forensic science?
> >
> > **Solution.** It amplifies tiny DNA samples from a crime scene into enough copies to analyse and match to a suspect.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe genetic engineering tools
- Explain PCR
- Weigh ethical issues

---

biology.A2.ecology-environment-depth.notes:
# Ecology & Environment at Depth

> [!intro] Biodiversity, conservation and human impact — data-driven, reusing statistics.

## Biodiversity and impact

Biodiversity underpins ecosystem stability; human activity (habitat loss, pollution, climate change) threatens it. Data and statistics quantify these trends.

## Conservation

Conservation weighs evidence and trade-offs to protect species and habitats — an applied, data-driven, and ethical challenge.

```formula Key facts
Biodiversity = genetic + species + ecosystem diversity
Human impacts: habitat loss, pollution, climate change
Use data/statistics to quantify change
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why does habitat loss reduce biodiversity so strongly?
> >
> > **Solution.** It removes the niches many species depend on, causing local extinctions and breaking food webs, which cascades to more losses.

## What you should be able to do

- Assess biodiversity
- Evaluate human impact
- Propose conservation strategies

---

biology.A2.evolution-depth.notes:
# Evolution at Depth

> [!intro] Speciation, molecular evidence and phylogenetics.

## Speciation

New species form when populations become reproductively isolated and diverge — often by geographic separation. This explains life's branching diversity.

## Molecular phylogenetics

Comparing DNA sequences reconstructs evolutionary relationships as trees. More similar sequences mean more recent common ancestors.

```formula Key facts
Speciation: reproductive isolation → divergence
More DNA similarity → more recent common ancestor
Phylogenetic trees show relationships
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** How does geographic isolation lead to a new species?
> >
> > **Solution.** Separated populations face different selection pressures and diverge until they can no longer interbreed — a new species.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain speciation
- Use molecular evidence
- Read phylogenetic trees

---

biology.A2.genetics-ii.subject: biology
biology.A2.genetics-ii.title: Genetics II
biology.A2.genetics-ii.summary: Linkage, mutation, genetic disorders and population genetics (Hardy-Weinberg).
biology.A2.genetics-ii.notes:
# Genetics II

> [!intro] Linkage, mutation, genetic disorders and population genetics (Hardy-Weinberg).

## Beyond simple inheritance

Genes on the same chromosome are linked; mutations change DNA, sometimes causing disorders. Real inheritance is richer than single-gene ratios.

## Population genetics

Hardy-Weinberg predicts allele frequencies in a stable population — reusing probability and algebra to study evolution quantitatively.

```formula Key facts
Linked genes are inherited together
Hardy–Weinberg: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, p + q = 1
Mutations are the source of new alleles
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** In a population, the recessive phenotype frequency q² = 0.16. Find q and p.
> >
> > **Solution.** q = √0.16 = 0.4. p = 1 − q = 0.6.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain linkage and mutation
- Analyse genetic disorders
- Apply Hardy-Weinberg

---

biology.A2.investigative-biology.notes:
# Investigative Biology Portfolio

> [!intro] Experimental design and data analysis — the capstone research strand.

## Experimental design

A good biology experiment controls variables, includes replicates and a control group, and defines what is measured — the basis of trustworthy results.

## Data analysis

Biological data is variable, so statistics (means, spread, significance) separate real effects from noise — reusing the maths statistics strand.

```formula Key facts
Control one variable; include a control group; replicate
Use statistics to test if a difference is real
Correlation ≠ causation
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** You find plant height correlates with soil nitrogen. Can you conclude nitrogen causes taller plants?
> >
> > **Solution.** Not from correlation alone — run a controlled experiment varying only nitrogen to test causation.

## What you should be able to do

- Design controlled experiments
- Analyse biological data
- Draw evidence-based conclusions

---

biology.F1.characteristics-classificatio.notes:
# What is Life? Characteristics & Classification

> [!intro] The characteristics shared by living things, and classification as an organising principle.

## Signs of life

Living things share features — movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition (MRS GREN). These distinguish life from non-life.

## Classification as a tool

Grouping organisms by shared features (not memorising a list) reveals relationships and makes the diversity of life manageable and predictable.

```formula Key facts
MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition
Classify from broad → specific by shared features
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Is a growing crystal alive? Use MRS GREN.
> >
> > **Solution.** A crystal grows but does not respire, reproduce, respond, excrete or feed. Since it fails MRS GREN, it is not living.

## What you should be able to do

- List the characteristics of life
- Explain why we classify organisms
- Use basic classification groups

---

biology.F1.living-environment-i.summary: Food chains and webs as energy flow, and how organisms depend on each other.
biology.F1.living-environment-i.notes:
# Living Things & Their Environment I

> [!intro] Food chains and webs as energy flow, and how organisms depend on each other.

## Energy flows through ecosystems

Food chains trace energy from producers (plants) to consumers. Energy is lost at each step, so chains are short — an ecological version of energy accounting.

## Interdependence

Organisms depend on each other and their environment; removing one affects many, shown by food webs linking multiple chains.

```formula Key facts
Food-chain arrows point in the direction of energy flow
Every chain begins with a producer
Energy is lost as heat at each level
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** In grass → grasshopper → frog, what is the producer and the primary consumer?
> >

# Nutrition & the Human Digestive System

> [!intro] Nutrients, a balanced diet, and how the digestive system breaks down food for energy.

biology.F1.the-cell.notes:
# The Cell

> [!intro] Cell theory, cell structure, and the differences between plant and animal cells.

## Cell theory

All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; cells come from pre-existing cells. This unifying model underlies all of biology.

## Structure and function

Organelles have jobs: the nucleus controls, mitochondria release energy, chloroplasts (plants) capture light. Plant cells add a wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

```formula Key facts
Cell theory: all life is cells; cell = basic unit; cells from cells
Plant extras: cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole
Nucleus controls; mitochondria release energy
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A cell has a wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Plant or animal?
> >
> > **Solution.** Plant cell — animal cells lack a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole.

## What you should be able to do

- State cell theory
- Identify cell structures
- Compare plant and animal cells

---

biology.F2.health-disease.notes:
# Health & Disease

> [!intro] Pathogens, how disease spreads, immunity and prevention.

## Pathogens

Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites cause infectious disease, spreading by air, water, contact or vectors. Understanding the route guides prevention.

## Immunity

The immune system recognises and destroys pathogens; vaccines train it in advance. Hygiene and vaccination are the front line of prevention.

```formula Key facts
Pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists
Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses
Vaccines create immune memory
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why won’t antibiotics cure a common cold?
> >
> > **Solution.** A cold is caused by a virus; antibiotics only act on bacteria, so they have no effect on the virus.

## What you should be able to do

- Identify types of pathogen
- Explain how disease spreads
- Describe immunity and prevention

---

# Human Physiology I

> [!intro] Respiration, circulation and transport as flow systems in the body.

## Breathing and respiration

Breathing brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide; cellular respiration then releases energy from glucose. The two are related but distinct.

The heart pumps blood through vessels to deliver oxygen and nutrients and remove waste — a transport network serving every cell.

```formula Key facts
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins toward it

```

> **Problem.** Why do arteries have thick, muscular walls?
> >
> > **Solution.** To withstand the high pressure of blood pumped directly from the heart, and to help maintain that pressure.

# Plant Biology I

> [!intro] Photosynthesis as energy capture, and transport in plants.

## Photosynthesis

Plants capture light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. This is the entry point of energy into most food chains.

## Plant transport

Xylem carries water up from roots; phloem carries sugars around the plant. Leaves are adapted (broad, thin, full of chloroplasts) to capture light.

```formula Key facts
Photosynthesis: CO₂ + H₂O —(light)→ glucose + O₂
Xylem carries water up; phloem carries sugars around
Leaves are broad and thin to capture light
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What raw materials and energy source does photosynthesis need, and what gas is released?
> >
> > **Solution.** It needs carbon dioxide, water and light energy; oxygen is released as a by-product.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe photosynthesis
- Explain transport in plants
- Relate leaves to their function

biology.F2.reproduction.notes:
# Reproduction

> [!intro] Asexual and sexual reproduction, and the human reproductive system.

## Two strategies

Asexual reproduction makes identical offspring from one parent (fast, no variation). Sexual reproduction combines two parents' genes, producing variation — the raw material for evolution.

## Human reproduction

Sexual reproduction in humans joins sperm and egg; the resulting variation is why siblings differ. This links directly to later genetics.

```formula Key facts
Asexual: 1 parent, identical offspring
Sexual: 2 parents, gametes, variation
Gametes carry half the genetic information
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why do offspring from sexual reproduction show variation?
> >
> > **Solution.** They combine genes from two parents; the random mix of maternal and paternal alleles produces new combinations.

## What you should be able to do

- Compare asexual and sexual reproduction
- Describe human reproduction
- Explain variation from sexual reproduction

---

biology.I1.cell-processes.notes:
# Cell Processes

> [!intro] Diffusion, osmosis and active transport — how substances cross membranes.

## Passive movement

Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration; osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane. Both are passive — no energy needed.

## Active transport

Moving substances against a concentration gradient needs energy (active transport). Cells use it to absorb nutrients even when scarce.

```formula Key facts
Diffusion/osmosis: high → low concentration (passive)
Osmosis = water across a membrane
Active transport: low → high, needs energy
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A cell is placed in pure water. Which way does water move and why?
> >
> > **Solution.** Water moves into the cell by osmosis — from high water potential (outside) to lower (inside), until balanced.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain diffusion and osmosis
- Describe active transport
- Relate transport to concentration

---

biology.I1.ecology-ecosystems.notes:
# Ecology & Ecosystems

> [!intro] Energy pyramids, nutrient cycles and population basics.

## Energy pyramids

Energy decreases up trophic levels (only ~10% passes on), so top predators are few. This explains pyramid shapes and short food chains.

## Cycles

Matter (carbon, nitrogen, water) cycles through ecosystems, unlike energy which flows through and is lost. Decomposers return nutrients to the soil.

```formula Key facts
~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level
Matter cycles; energy flows and is lost
Decomposers recycle nutrients
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** If producers capture 10000 kJ, roughly how much reaches a secondary consumer?
> >
> > **Solution.** ~10% per level: producer 10000 → primary 1000 → secondary ~100 kJ.

## What you should be able to do

- Interpret energy pyramids
- Describe nutrient cycles
- Explain population change

---

biology.I1.enzymes.notes:
# Enzymes

> [!intro] Enzymes as biological catalysts, and the factors that affect their activity.

## Biological catalysts

Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy, binding substrates at an active site (lock-and-key). They are not used up — reusing the catalyst idea from chemistry.

## Sensitive to conditions

Temperature and pH affect enzyme shape; too much denatures them permanently. Each enzyme has an optimum, explaining why body temperature matters.

```formula Key facts
Enzymes lower activation energy (biological catalysts)
Each has an optimum temperature and pH
High heat / extreme pH denatures (permanent)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why does an enzyme stop working when boiled?
> >
> > **Solution.** Heat denatures it — the active site changes shape permanently, so the substrate no longer fits.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain enzyme action
- Describe factors affecting enzymes
- Relate enzymes to reaction rate

---

biology.I1.human-physiology-ii.notes:
# Human Physiology II

> [!intro] Nervous and endocrine coordination, and homeostasis as feedback control.

## Two control systems

The nervous system sends fast electrical signals; the endocrine system sends slower, longer-lasting hormones. Together they coordinate the body.

## Homeostasis

The body keeps internal conditions stable (temperature, glucose) using negative feedback — deviations trigger corrections, like a thermostat.

```formula Key facts
Nervous control: fast, brief (electrical)
Hormonal control: slower, longer (chemical)
Negative feedback opposes the change (homeostasis)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Blood glucose rises after a meal. How does negative feedback restore it?
> >
> > **Solution.** The pancreas releases insulin, which makes cells take up glucose, lowering blood glucose back to normal.

## What you should be able to do

- Compare nervous and hormonal control
- Explain homeostasis
- Describe negative feedback

---

biology.I1.respiration-photosynthesis.notes:
# Respiration & Photosynthesis (Biochemical)

> [!intro] The energy budgets of respiration and photosynthesis, quantitatively.

## Two complementary processes

Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose; respiration releases it. They are near-opposites, and together drive energy flow through ecosystems.

## Aerobic vs anaerobic

Aerobic respiration (with oxygen) releases much more energy than anaerobic. The equations reveal the reactants and products precisely.

```formula Key facts
Aerobic: glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy
Anaerobic releases less energy
Photosynthesis ≈ the reverse of respiration
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why does aerobic respiration release more energy than anaerobic?
> >
> > **Solution.** With oxygen, glucose is fully broken down to CO₂ and water; without it, glucose is only partially broken down.

## What you should be able to do

- Write respiration and photosynthesis equations
- Compare the two processes

biology.I2.evolution-natural-selection.notes:
# Evolution & Natural Selection

> [!intro] The unifying theory of biology: evidence and mechanism of natural selection.

## Natural selection

Individuals vary; those better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, passing on their traits. Over generations, populations adapt.

## The unifying theory

Evolution explains the diversity and relatedness of life. Evidence comes from fossils, anatomy, and DNA — a single framework for all biology.

```formula Key facts
Variation + selection + inheritance + time → evolution
Selection acts on populations, not individuals
Evidence: fossils, anatomy, DNA
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** How does antibiotic resistance in bacteria illustrate natural selection?
> >
> > **Solution.** Random variation makes some bacteria resistant; the antibiotic kills the rest; survivors reproduce, so the population becomes resistant.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain natural selection
- Cite evidence for evolution
- Relate variation to adaptation

---

# Genetics I: Inheritance

> [!intro] Mendel's laws and monohybrid/dihybrid crosses — genetics as probability.

## Genes come in pairs

Each trait has two alleles, one from each parent; dominant alleles mask recessive ones. Mendel discovered these inheritance patterns from breeding experiments.

## Genetics is probability

Punnett squares predict offspring ratios (like 3:1) — this is exactly the probability from maths applied to inheritance, an interleaving in action.

```formula Key facts
Dominant allele masks recessive
Genotype = alleles; phenotype = appearance
Aa × Aa → 3 : 1 phenotype ratio
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt) are crossed. What fraction of offspring are short (tt)?
> >
> > **Solution.** Punnett square Tt × Tt → TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Short (tt) = 1/4 of offspring.

## What you should be able to do

- Use Mendelian ratios

- Explain dominant and recessive alleles

# Population Biology

> [!intro] Exponential and logistic growth, and what limits populations.

## Growth models

Unchecked populations grow exponentially; real ones level off (logistic) as resources limit them at the carrying capacity — reusing exponentials from maths.

## Limiting factors

Food, space, predators and disease limit growth. Understanding them predicts population dynamics and informs conservation.

```formula Key facts
Unlimited growth is exponential
Real populations level at the carrying capacity (logistic)
Limiting factors: food, space, predators, disease
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why does a population stop growing exponentially in the wild?
> >
> > **Solution.** Resources (food, space) become limiting and predation/disease rise, so the population levels off at the carrying capacity.

chemistry.A1.chemical-equilibrium.summary: Equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the reaction quotient Q, and ICE-table calculations.
chemistry.A1.chemical-equilibrium.notes:
# Chemical Equilibrium (Quantitative)

> [!intro] Equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the reaction quotient Q, and ICE-table calculations.

## Equilibrium constant

Kc = [products]/[reactants], each raised to its coefficient (pure solids/liquids omitted). Large K favours products. Kp uses partial pressures.

## Q vs K and ICE tables

The reaction quotient Q has K's form but at any moment. Q < K → forward; Q > K → backward. ICE (Initial–Change–Equilibrium) tables organise the algebra.

```formula Key formulas
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD :  Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b
Q < K → forward; Q > K → backward; Q = K → equilibrium
Kp = Kc (RT)^(Δn_gas)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, at equilibrium [H₂]=[I₂]=0.10 M and [HI]=0.80 M. Find Kc.
> >
> > **Solution.** Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = (0.80)² / (0.10×0.10) = 0.64/0.01 = 64. K ≫ 1 → products favoured.

## What you should be able to do

- Write Kc/Kp expressions
- Use Q to predict direction
- Solve equilibria with ICE tables

---

chemistry.A1.chemical-kinetics.notes:
# Chemical Kinetics

> [!intro] Rate laws, order of reaction, half-life and the Arrhenius temperature dependence.

## Rate laws and order

Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n where m, n (the orders) are found by experiment, not from the equation. Overall order is m+n; units of k depend on the order.

## Arrhenius

k = A e^(−Eₐ/RT): rate constant rises with temperature and falls with activation energy. Logs give ln k = ln A − Eₐ/RT — a straight line (reusing logarithms).

```formula Key formulas
Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n  (m, n from experiment)
First-order half-life: t½ = 0.693 / k
Arrhenius: k = A e^(−Eₐ/RT);  ln k = ln A − Eₐ/RT
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 s⁻¹. Find its half-life.
> >
> > **Solution.** t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 s. First-order half-life is constant, independent of starting concentration.

## What you should be able to do

- Write and use rate laws
- Determine order experimentally
- Apply the Arrhenius relationship

---

chemistry.A1.chemical-thermodynamics.notes:
# Chemical Thermodynamics

> [!intro] Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy — the thermodynamic criterion for whether a reaction is spontaneous.

## Enthalpy and entropy

Enthalpy (ΔH) tracks heat exchanged; entropy (ΔS) tracks disorder. Reactions are favoured by releasing energy (ΔH<0) and increasing disorder (ΔS>0).

## Gibbs free energy

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides spontaneity: ΔG < 0 spontaneous, = 0 at equilibrium, > 0 non-spontaneous. The T term means some reactions become spontaneous only above/below a certain temperature.

```formula Key formulas
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS  (T in kelvin)
ΔG < 0 spontaneous; = 0 equilibrium; > 0 non-spontaneous
ΔG° = −RT ln K
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +0.100 kJ/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it spontaneous?
> >
> > **Solution.** Spontaneous when ΔH − TΔS < 0 → T > ΔH/ΔS = 40/0.100 = 400 K. So spontaneous above 400 K.

## What you should be able to do

- Use enthalpy and entropy changes
- Apply ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
- Predict spontaneity and its temperature dependence

---

chemistry.A1.electrochemistry.notes:
# Electrochemistry

> [!intro] Galvanic and electrolytic cells, cell potentials, the Nernst equation and Faraday's laws of electrolysis.

## Cells from redox

A galvanic cell turns a spontaneous redox reaction into electricity: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; positive → spontaneous.

## Electrolysis and Faraday

An electrolytic cell uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. Amount deposited follows Faraday: moles of electrons = charge ÷ F, F ≈ 96500 C/mol.

```formula Key formulas
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode  (>0 → spontaneous)
ΔG° = −nFE°cell
Faraday: moles e⁻ = Q/F,  Q = I×t,  F ≈ 96500 C/mol
Nernst: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A current of 2 A flows for 965 s through molten NaCl. How many moles of electrons pass?
> >
> > **Solution.** Q = I×t = 2 × 965 = 1930 C. Moles e⁻ = Q/F = 1930/96500 = 0.02 mol — deposits 0.02 mol Na at the cathode.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe galvanic and electrolytic cells
- Use standard electrode potentials
- Apply Faraday's laws

---

chemistry.A1.ionic-equilibrium.summary: pH of strong and weak acids, buffers (Henderson–Hasselbalch), and the solubility product Ksp.
chemistry.A1.ionic-equilibrium.notes:
# Ionic Equilibrium

> [!intro] pH of strong and weak acids, buffers (Henderson–Hasselbalch), and the solubility product Ksp.

## Weak acids and Ka

Strong acids dissociate fully; weak acids only partially, described by Ka. For a weak acid, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C).

## Buffers and Ksp

A buffer (weak acid + its salt) resists pH change: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). The solubility product Ksp sets the maximum ionic product of a sparingly soluble salt.

```formula Key formulas
pH = −log[H⁺];  Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10^(−14) at 25°C
Weak acid: [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C)
Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])
Ksp = [cation]^x[anion]^y at saturation
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Find the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵).
> >
> > **Solution.** [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C) = √(1.8×10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = √(1.8×10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.34×10⁻³. pH = −log(1.34×10⁻³) ≈ 2.87.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate pH of strong/weak acids
- Use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
- Apply Ksp to solubility

---

chemistry.A1.periodic-properties.summary: Trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity, explained by nuclear charge and shielding.
outcomes: Compare elements across periods and groups
chemistry.A1.periodic-properties.notes:
# Periodic Properties & s/p-Block

> [!intro] Trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity, explained by nuclear charge and shielding.

## Trends from effective nuclear charge

Across a period, more protons pull the same shell in → atoms shrink, ionisation energy and electronegativity rise. Down a group, extra shells and shielding → atoms grow, ionisation energy falls.

## Block chemistry

The s-block (reactive metals, +1/+2 ions) and p-block (non-metals, metalloids, varied) show patterns explained by valence configuration.

```formula Key formulas
Across a period →: radius ↓, ionisation energy ↑, electronegativity ↑
Down a group ↓: radius ↑, ionisation energy ↓
Effective nuclear charge ≈ protons − shielding
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Which has the larger atomic radius: Na or Cl? Why?
> >
> > **Solution.** Na. Both are Period 3, but Cl has more protons pulling the same shell in (higher effective nuclear charge), so Cl is smaller — radius decreases across a period.

chemistry.A2.analytical-chemistry.notes:
# Analytical & Practical Chemistry Portfolio

> [!intro] Qualitative and quantitative analysis (including titration calculations) and treatment of experimental error — the capstone lab strand.

## Identifying and measuring

Qualitative analysis identifies what is present (flame tests, precipitates, gas tests); quantitative analysis measures how much (titration, gravimetry).

## Titration calculations

From a titration, moles of one reactant give moles of the other via the equation, then concentration. Repeat for concordant results and report uncertainty.

```formula Key formulas
n = C × V (V in litres)
At the end point: n(acid)/n(base) = mole ratio from the equation
Concordant titres agree within ~0.10 cm³
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** 25.0 cm³ of NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 M HCl (1:1). Find the NaOH concentration.
> >
> > **Solution.** n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol. 1:1 → n(NaOH) = 0.00200 mol. C = n/V = 0.00200/0.0250 = 0.080 M.

## What you should be able to do

- Perform qualitative tests
- Carry out titration calculations
- Treat experimental uncertainty

---

# Biomolecules & Polymers

> [!intro] Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and polymers — the chemistry underlying biology.

## Biomolecules

Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids are built from small repeating monomers (sugars, amino acids, nucleotides) joined by condensation (losing water).

## Polymers

Polymers are long chains of monomers — natural (proteins, starch, DNA) or synthetic (polythene, PVC). Addition polymers form from alkenes; condensation polymers release a small molecule per link.

```formula Key formulas
Condensation: monomer + monomer → dimer + H₂O
Addition: n(CH₂=CH₂) → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–
Proteins = polymers of amino acids (peptide bonds)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What type of polymerisation forms polythene from ethene, and what small molecule (if any) is lost?
> >
> > **Solution.** Addition polymerisation: the C=C bonds open and monomers add with no small molecule lost. n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe major biomolecules
- Explain condensation and addition polymerisation
- Connect structure to function

---

chemistry.A2.coordination-chemistry.notes:
# d-Block & Coordination Chemistry

> [!intro] Transition-metal properties, complex ions, ligands, coordination number and the origin of colour.

## Transition metals

d-block elements show variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic activity — all from partly filled d-orbitals.

## Complexes and colour

A central metal ion bonds to ligands (electron-pair donors); the number of donor atoms is the coordination number. Ligands split the d-orbitals in energy; electrons absorbing specific wavelengths to jump the gap produce colour.

```formula Key formulas
Coordination number = number of ligand donor atoms
Ligand = electron-pair (Lewis base) donor
Colour arises from d–d electron transitions (orbital splitting)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** In [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, what is the coordination number and why is it coloured?
> >
> > **Solution.** Six water ligands → coordination number 6. They split Cu²⁺'s 3d orbitals; a d-electron absorbs part of visible light to jump the gap, so the complex appears blue.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe transition-metal properties
- Interpret coordination complexes
- Relate d-electrons to colour and catalysis

---

# Functional-Group Chemistry

> [!intro] Alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and amines — characteristic reactions and interconversions.

## Groups define reactivity

Each functional group has signature reactions: alcohols oxidise, carboxylic acids neutralise bases, amines act as weak bases. Identify the group and you predict the chemistry.

## Oxidation ladder

Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid on oxidation; secondary alcohol → ketone (no further). These routes build target molecules.

```formula Key formulas
–OH alcohol, –CHO aldehyde, C=O ketone, –COOH acid, –NH₂ amine
Primary alcohol —[O]→ aldehyde —[O]→ carboxylic acid
Secondary alcohol —[O]→ ketone (stops)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What is formed when ethanol (a primary alcohol) is fully oxidised?
> >
> > **Solution.** Ethanol → ethanal (aldehyde) → ethanoic acid. Full oxidation gives the carboxylic acid, ethanoic (acetic) acid.

## What you should be able to do

- Recognise major functional groups
- Predict characteristic reactions
- Plan functional-group interconversions

---

chemistry.A2.organic-mechanisms.notes:
# Organic Reaction Mechanisms

> [!intro] Nucleophiles, electrophiles, curly-arrow mechanisms and the major pathways — reasoned, not memorised.

## Electron flow

Organic reactions are electrons moving from electron-rich (nucleophile) to electron-poor (electrophile) sites. Curly arrows show electron-pair movement, always starting from a lone pair or bond.

## Major pathways

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2), electrophilic addition (to C=C), and elimination. Understanding the pathway predicts products instead of memorising thousands of reactions.

```formula Key formulas
Curly arrow: starts from an electron pair (lone pair or bond)
Nucleophile = electron-pair donor (electron-rich)
Electrophile = electron-pair acceptor (electron-poor)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** In OH⁻ + CH₃Br, identify the nucleophile and product.
> >
> > **Solution.** OH⁻ is the electron-rich nucleophile; it attacks the electron-poor carbon bonded to Br, displacing Br⁻ (nucleophilic substitution). Product: CH₃OH.

## What you should be able to do

- Identify nucleophiles and electrophiles
- Follow substitution/addition/elimination mechanisms
- Predict products by electron flow

---

chemistry.F1.matter-particles-states.notes:
# Matter, Particles & States

> [!intro] The particle (kinetic-molecular) model of matter, the three states, and changes of state — the microscopic picture behind all of chemistry.

## Everything is particles in motion

All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules, ions) in constant motion. Their spacing, arrangement and energy decide the state: solids (fixed, vibrating), liquids (close, sliding), gases (far apart, fast, free).

## Changes of state are energy changes

Heating supplies energy that overcomes the forces holding particles together — melting then boiling. During a state change the temperature stays constant (energy goes into breaking forces, not raising KE). Mass is always conserved.

## Interparticle forces set properties

Stronger interparticle forces mean higher melting and boiling points. This single idea (developed further in bonding) explains why ionic solids melt high and gases condense low.

```formula Key formulas
Solid → Liquid → Gas : particle energy and spacing increase
During melting/boiling: temperature constant (latent heat breaks forces)
Mass conserved in every physical change
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why does the temperature stay constant while ice melts at 0°C even though heat is being added?
> >
> > **Solution.** The added energy (latent heat of fusion) breaks the forces holding water molecules in the rigid ice lattice, not raising their kinetic energy. Temperature (a measure of average KE) stays at 0°C until all the ice has melted.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe matter using the kinetic-particle model
- Explain the three states and changes between them by particle arrangement and energy
- Distinguish pure substances from mixtures

---

chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.notes:
# Physical vs Chemical Change

> [!intro] Telling physical from chemical changes, the evidence of reaction, and conservation of mass as the accounting law behind balancing.

## Two kinds of change

A physical change alters form but not the substance (melting, dissolving); a chemical change makes new substances (burning, rusting), often signalled by colour change, gas, heat/light, or a precipitate.

## Conservation of mass

Atoms are only rearranged in a reaction, so total mass of reactants = total mass of products. In an open system, escaping gas can make mass appear to fall — account for it.

```formula Key formulas
Total mass of reactants = total mass of products
mass(products) − mass(reactants) = 0 (closed system)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** 4 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 32 g of oxygen. What mass of water forms?
> >
> > **Solution.** By conservation of mass, mass of water = 4 + 32 = 36 g. Atoms are only rearranged into H₂O.

## What you should be able to do

- Distinguish physical and chemical changes
- Identify signs of a chemical reaction
- Apply conservation of mass quantitatively

---

chemistry.F1.separation-techniques.notes:
# Separation Techniques

> [!intro] Filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography — separating mixtures by exploiting differences in physical properties.

## Separate by difference

Mixtures separate because components differ — particle size (filtration), boiling point (distillation), or affinity for a moving vs stationary phase (chromatography).

## Chromatography and Rf

In paper chromatography, components travel different distances. The retention factor Rf = (distance moved by spot)/(distance moved by solvent) identifies a component and is always between 0 and 1.

```formula Key formulas
Rf = (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent front)
0 ≤ Rf ≤ 1
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A pigment spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent front moves 12.0 cm. Find its Rf.
> >
> > **Solution.** Rf = 3.0 / 12.0 = 0.25. Being < 1 and characteristic under those conditions, it helps identify the pigment.

## What you should be able to do

- Choose a separation method from the property that differs
- Explain distillation and chromatography
- Interpret a chromatogram (Rf)

---

chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.notes:
# Atomic Structure I

> [!intro] Protons, neutrons and electrons; atomic number, mass number, isotopes and relative atomic mass.

## Inside the atom

A tiny dense nucleus of protons (+1) and neutrons (0) is surrounded by electrons (−1). The atomic number Z (protons) defines the element; a neutral atom has equal protons and electrons.

## Isotopes and relative atomic mass

Isotopes are atoms of one element with different neutron numbers — same chemistry, different mass. Relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of isotope masses, which is why it is rarely a whole number.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 320 170" role="img" aria-label="Atom with nucleus and two electron shells" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <circle cx="160" cy="80" r="68" fill="none" stroke="#39466a"/>
  <circle cx="160" cy="80" r="42" fill="none" stroke="#39466a"/>
  <circle cx="160" cy="80" r="15" fill="#6366f1"/>
  <text x="160" y="84" font-size="9" fill="#fff" text-anchor="middle">nucleus</text>
  <circle cx="228" cy="80" r="5" fill="#6ee7a8"/><circle cx="92" cy="80" r="5" fill="#6ee7a8"/>
  <circle cx="160" cy="38" r="5" fill="#a8c0ff"/><circle cx="160" cy="122" r="5" fill="#a8c0ff"/>
  <circle cx="202" cy="38" r="5" fill="#a8c0ff"/>
  <text x="160" y="165" font-size="10" fill="#9aa8c4" text-anchor="middle">protons + neutrons in the nucleus; electrons in shells</text>
</svg>
```

```formula Key formulas
Atomic number Z = protons = electrons (neutral atom)
Mass number A = protons + neutrons
Neutrons = A − Z
Relative atomic mass = Σ(isotope mass × fractional abundance)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl. Find its relative atomic mass.
> >
> > **Solution.** Ar = 35(0.75) + 37(0.25) = 26.25 + 9.25 = 35.5. This weighted average is why chlorine's Ar is 35.5, not a whole number.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe subatomic particles and their charges
- Use atomic number and mass number
- Explain isotopes and compute relative atomic mass

---

chemistry.F2.chemical-formulae-equations.notes:
# Chemical Formulae & Equations

> [!intro] Writing formulae from valency and balancing equations as the visible bookkeeping of conservation of mass.

## Formulae from valency

A formula shows which atoms combine and in what ratio, set by combining power (valency). Swap-and-drop the valencies (e.g., Al³⁺ and O²⁻ → Al₂O₃).

## Balancing = conservation

A balanced equation has equal atoms of each element on both sides because atoms are conserved. Only coefficients (amounts) are adjusted — never subscripts.

```formula Key formulas
Atoms of each element: reactant side = product side
Coefficients give the mole ratio of the reaction
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Balance: Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃.
> >
> > **Solution.** 4 Al + 3 O₂ → 2 Al₂O₃. Check: Al 4=4, O 6=6. Adjust coefficients only.

## What you should be able to do

- Write formulae from valencies
- Balance chemical equations
- Interpret an equation in moles

chemistry.F2.mole-concept.notes:
# The Mole Concept

> [!intro] The mole, Avogadro's number and molar mass — proportional reasoning applied to counting particles. The keystone of all quantitative chemistry.

## Counting by weighing

Atoms are too small to count, so we weigh them. One mole is Avogadro's number (Nₐ ≈ 6.022×10²³) of particles; the molar mass in g/mol equals the relative atomic/molecular mass, linking mass to particle count.

## The mole is a ratio

moles = mass ÷ molar mass — the same proportional reasoning as ratios, now applied to particles. Every stoichiometry, concentration and gas calculation flows from this.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 120" role="img" aria-label="Mass to moles to particles conversion" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect x="16" y="30" width="86" height="60" rx="8" fill="#12182a" stroke="#39466a"/>
  <rect x="127" y="30" width="86" height="60" rx="8" fill="#12182a" stroke="#39466a"/>
  <rect x="238" y="30" width="86" height="60" rx="8" fill="#12182a" stroke="#39466a"/>
  <text x="59" y="58" font-size="13" fill="#e6ecff" text-anchor="middle">mass (g)</text>
  <text x="170" y="58" font-size="13" fill="#8fa0ff" text-anchor="middle">moles n</text>
  <text x="281" y="58" font-size="13" fill="#6ee7a8" text-anchor="middle">particles</text>
  <line x1="102" y1="60" x2="127" y2="60" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#a)"/>
  <line x1="213" y1="60" x2="238" y2="60" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#a)"/>
  <text x="114" y="24" font-size="9" fill="#9aa8c4" text-anchor="middle">÷ M</text>
  <text x="225" y="24" font-size="9" fill="#9aa8c4" text-anchor="middle">× Nₐ</text>
  <defs><marker id="a" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#6366f1"/></marker></defs>
</svg>
```

```formula Key formulas
n = m / M   (moles = mass ÷ molar mass)
Number of particles = n × Nₐ,   Nₐ ≈ 6.022×10^23 /mol
Molar mass of a compound = Σ (atomic masses)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** How many water molecules are in 36 g of water? (M = 18 g/mol)
> >
> > **Solution.** n = m/M = 36/18 = 2 mol. Molecules = n × Nₐ = 2 × 6.022×10²³ = 1.2×10²⁴ molecules.

## What you should be able to do

- Define the mole and Avogadro's number
- Convert between mass, moles and number of particles
- Compute molar mass of compounds

---

chemistry.F2.periodic-table.notes:
# The Periodic Table as a Map

> [!intro] Periods and groups as patterns arising from electron configuration — a predictive map, not a list to memorise.

## A map from electron structure

Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number into periods (rows) and groups (columns). Group number equals the number of outer (valence) electrons, which is why a group shares chemistry.

## Trends are predictable

Reactivity, atomic size and metallic character change smoothly across periods and down groups — Group 1 metals get more reactive down the group; Group 17 non-metals less reactive down.

```formula Key formulas
Group number (main groups) = number of valence electrons
Period number = number of occupied electron shells
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Element in Group 2, Period 3. How many valence electrons and shells, and what is it?
> >
> > **Solution.** 2 valence electrons and 3 shells → magnesium (Mg). Its 2 outer electrons make it a reactive Group-2 metal forming Mg²⁺.

## What you should be able to do

- Read the periodic table's layout
- Relate group number to valence electrons
- Predict reactivity trends

---

chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.notes:
# Introductory Stoichiometry

> [!intro] Using mole ratios from balanced equations for mass-to-mass calculations, and finding the limiting reactant.

## Coefficients are mole ratios

The coefficients of a balanced equation give the ratio of moles reacting. To go grams-to-grams: convert to moles, apply the mole ratio, convert back to mass.

## Limiting reactant

The reactant that runs out first caps the product. Compare moles ÷ coefficient for each reactant; the smallest is limiting.

```formula Key formulas
mass → n = m/M → ×(mole ratio) → m = n×M
Limiting reactant: smallest of (moles ÷ coefficient)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ from 2 mol N₂ with excess H₂?
> >
> > **Solution.** Mole ratio N₂ : NH₃ = 1 : 2, so 2 mol N₂ → 4 mol NH₃ (H₂ excess, N₂ limiting).

## What you should be able to do

- Use mole ratios from equations
- Perform mass → mole → mole → mass calculations
- Identify the limiting reactant

---

chemistry.I1.acids-bases-salts.notes:
# Acids, Bases & Salts

> [!intro] The pH scale as a logarithm of H⁺ concentration, neutralisation, and titration.

## Acids, bases and pH

Acids donate H⁺ (Brønsted); bases accept H⁺ (or donate OH⁻). pH = −log[H⁺] compresses a huge range into 0–14; each unit is a ten-fold change in acidity.

## Neutralisation and titration

Acid + base → salt + water. Titration finds an unknown concentration by adding a standard solution to the equivalence point, using n = CV.

```formula Key formulas
pH = −log[H⁺],  [H⁺] = 10^(−pH)
At 25°C: [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0×10^(−14)
Acid + base → salt + water
Titration: n = C × V
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A solution has [H⁺] = 1×10⁻³ mol/L. Find its pH and state if it is acidic.
> >
> > **Solution.** pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3. Since pH < 7, the solution is acidic.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe acids and bases (Arrhenius/Brønsted)
- Use the pH scale quantitatively
- Explain neutralisation and titration

---

chemistry.I1.bonding-i.notes:
# Bonding I

> [!intro] Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding from the drive for full outer shells, and how bonding type dictates properties.

## Atoms bond for stable octets

Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a full outer shell. Metal + non-metal transfer → ionic; non-metals share → covalent; metals pool a "sea" of delocalised electrons → metallic.

## Bonding sets properties

Ionic solids form giant lattices (high melting, conduct when molten/aqueous); covalent molecules are often low-melting and non-conducting; metals conduct and are malleable via mobile electrons.

```formula Key formulas
Ionic: metal (loses e⁻) + non-metal (gains e⁻) → ions
Covalent: shared electron pair between non-metals
Metallic: cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Predict the bonding and a property of MgCl₂.
> >
> > **Solution.** Mg transfers 2 electrons to two Cl → Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻: ionic. Property: high melting point; conducts when molten/dissolved (mobile ions).

## What you should be able to do

- Distinguish ionic, covalent, metallic bonds
- Draw electron-dot (Lewis) structures
- Relate bonding to physical properties

---

chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.notes:
# Rates of Reaction

> [!intro] Collision theory and the factors that change reaction rate, read from rate graphs.

## Collision theory

Reactions occur when particles collide with energy ≥ activation energy and correct orientation. Concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts increase the frequency or success of collisions.

## Rate from graphs

Rate = Δ[concentration] ÷ time = the gradient of a concentration-vs-time graph — steep at first, flattening as reactants deplete. Rate-as-slope, shared with physics and calculus.

```formula Key formulas
Rate = Δ[concentration] / Δt = gradient of the curve
Higher T, [conc], surface area, or a catalyst → faster
Catalyst lowers activation energy Eₐ (not consumed)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A reaction produces 20 cm³ of gas in the first 10 s, then slows. Average rate over that interval?
> >
> > **Solution.** Average rate = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 cm³/s. It slows later as reactant concentration falls, reducing collision frequency.

## What you should be able to do

- Identify factors affecting rate
- Interpret rate graphs
- Explain rate with collision theory and activation energy

---

chemistry.I1.reactions-equations.notes:
# Reactions & Equations Deepened

> [!intro] Reaction types, net ionic equations, oxidation numbers and the essentials of redox.

## Types of reaction

Combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement (precipitation/neutralisation). The type predicts the products.

## Redox by electron transfer

Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain (OIL RIG). Oxidation numbers track it: the species whose oxidation number rises is oxidised; the oxidising agent is itself reduced.

```formula Key formulas
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)
Oxidation number ↑ = oxidised; ↓ = reduced
Net ionic equation: cancel spectator ions
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is oxidised?
> >
> > **Solution.** Zn: 0 → +2 (loses electrons) → oxidised (reducing agent). Cu²⁺: +2 → 0 (gains electrons) → reduced.

## What you should be able to do

- Classify reaction types
- Write net ionic equations
- Assign oxidation numbers and identify redox

---

chemistry.I1.solutions-concentration.notes:
# Solutions & Concentration

> [!intro] Molarity, dilution and the mole concept applied to real solutions.

## Concentration as a rate

Molarity (M) is moles of solute per litre of solution — again a ratio, bridging the mole concept to practical lab quantities.

## Dilution conserves moles

Adding solvent lowers concentration but keeps moles of solute fixed: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ — inverse proportion in action.

```formula Key formulas
Molarity M = n / V(litres)
n = M × V
Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What volume of 2 M stock makes 250 mL of 0.5 M solution?
> >
> > **Solution.** C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ → 2 × V₁ = 0.5 × 0.250 → V₁ = 0.0625 L = 62.5 mL, then dilute to 250 mL.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate molarity
- Perform dilution calculations
- Relate concentration, moles and volume

---

chemistry.I2.atomic-structure-ii.notes:
# Atomic Structure II

> [!intro] Electron configuration, subshells and quantum shells — the origin of the periodic table's shape.

## Electrons fill by energy

Electrons occupy shells and subshells (s, p, d) in order of increasing energy (aufbau). Configuration like 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ (Na) explains an element's group and reactivity.

## Valence controls chemistry

The outer-shell configuration determines bonding. Noble gases have full shells (unreactive); Group 1 has one easily-lost outer electron.

```formula Key formulas
Shell capacity = 2n² electrons (n = shell number)
Filling order (aufbau): 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d ...
Valence electrons = electrons in the outermost shell
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Write the electron configuration of sodium (Z = 11) and give its group.
> >
> > **Solution.** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. One valence electron in shell 3 → Group 1, Period 3. That 3s electron is easily lost to form Na⁺.

## What you should be able to do

- Write electron configurations (up to ~Z=20)
- Relate configuration to periodic position
- Explain shell energies intuitively

---

chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.notes:
# Bonding II

> [!intro] Molecular shapes from VSEPR, bond and molecular polarity, and intermolecular forces.

## Shape from electron-pair repulsion

Electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom repel and spread as far apart as possible (VSEPR): 2 pairs → linear (180°), 3 → trigonal (120°), 4 → tetrahedral (109.5°); lone pairs bend the shape.

## Polarity and intermolecular forces

Unequal sharing makes polar bonds; symmetry decides overall polarity. Intermolecular forces (London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding) set boiling points and solubility.

```formula Key formulas
VSEPR: 2 pairs → 180°, 3 → 120°, 4 → 109.5°
Strength: London dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bond
Symmetric shape can be non-polar despite polar bonds (CO₂)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Predict the shape and polarity of CO₂ and of H₂O.
> >
> > **Solution.** CO₂: 2 bonding regions, no lone pairs on C → linear (180°); dipoles cancel → non-polar. H₂O: 2 bonding + 2 lone pairs → bent (~104.5°); dipoles do not cancel → polar (and hydrogen-bonds).

## What you should be able to do

- Predict shapes with VSEPR
- Determine molecular polarity
- Rank intermolecular forces

---

chemistry.I2.energetics.subject: chemistry
chemistry.I2.energetics.title: Energetics (Thermochemistry)
chemistry.I2.energetics.summary: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, enthalpy change, bond energies and Hess's law.
chemistry.I2.energetics.notes:
# Energetics (Thermochemistry)

> [!intro] Exothermic and endothermic reactions, enthalpy change, bond energies and Hess's law.

## Enthalpy change

Reactions release energy (exothermic, ΔH negative) or absorb it (endothermic, ΔH positive). Breaking bonds costs energy; making bonds releases it.

## Bond energies and Hess

ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made). Hess's law: total ΔH is the same by any route (energy is conserved), so you can add known steps to find an unknown ΔH.

```formula Key formulas
ΔH < 0 exothermic; ΔH > 0 endothermic
ΔH ≈ Σ(bond energies broken) − Σ(bond energies made)
Hess's law: ΔH is route-independent (add steps)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, broken: H–H(436) + Cl–Cl(242); made: 2×H–Cl(431) kJ/mol. Find ΔH.
> >
> > **Solution.** ΔH = (436 + 242) − (2×431) = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol → exothermic.

## What you should be able to do

- Classify reactions by ΔH sign
- Estimate ΔH from bond energies
- Apply Hess's law

---

chemistry.I2.equilibrium-intro.summary: Dynamic equilibrium, the equilibrium constant, and Le Chatelier's principle.
chemistry.I2.equilibrium-intro.notes:
# Quantitative Equilibrium (Introduction)

> [!intro] Dynamic equilibrium, the equilibrium constant, and Le Chatelier's principle.

## Dynamic equilibrium

In a reversible reaction, equilibrium is reached when forward and backward rates are equal — concentrations stay constant though reaction continues.

## Le Chatelier

Disturb an equilibrium (concentration, temperature, pressure) and it shifts to oppose the change. Adding reactant or removing product shifts toward products.

```formula Key formulas
At equilibrium: forward rate = backward rate
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD :  K = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b
Le Chatelier: system shifts to oppose the imposed change
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic), how does increasing pressure affect NH₃ yield?
> >
> > **Solution.** Higher pressure shifts equilibrium to fewer gas moles (4 → 2), i.e., toward NH₃ — the basis of the Haber process.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain dynamic equilibrium
- Write an equilibrium expression
- Predict shifts with Le Chatelier

---

chemistry.I2.gas-laws-kinetic-theory.notes:
# Gas Laws & Kinetic Theory

> [!intro] Boyle's, Charles's and the combined/ideal gas laws, grounded in kinetic theory. Shared with physics.

## The gas laws

For a fixed amount of gas, P, V and T are linked: Boyle (PV constant at fixed T), Charles (V/T constant at fixed P), combined P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. Adding amount gives PV = nRT.

## Kinetic theory

A gas is many particles in fast random motion; pressure is their wall collisions, and temperature (in kelvin) is proportional to average kinetic energy.

```formula Key formulas
PV = nRT,  R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (const T)
Charles: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (const P)
Combined: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ (T in kelvin)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A gas occupies 2.0 L at 300 K. What volume at 450 K, constant pressure?
> >
> > **Solution.** Charles: 2.0/300 = V₂/450 → V₂ = 2.0 × (450/300) = 3.0 L. (Use kelvin.)

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the individual and combined gas laws
- Use PV = nRT
- Relate macroscopic behaviour to particle motion

---

chemistry.I2.organic-intro.notes:
# Introductory Organic Chemistry

> [!intro] The chemistry of carbon: hydrocarbons, functional groups, homologous series and IUPAC naming.

## Carbon's versatility

Carbon forms four covalent bonds and chains/rings with itself (catenation), giving millions of compounds. Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) are saturated; alkenes have a C=C double bond.

## Functional groups & naming

A functional group (–OH, –COOH, C=C) is the reactive site defining a molecule's chemistry. IUPAC names use the longest carbon chain (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) plus a suffix for the group.

```formula Key formulas
Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (saturated, single bonds)
Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ (one C=C double bond)
Chain roots: meth(1), eth(2), prop(3), but(4)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Give the molecular formula of the alkane with 3 carbons, and name it.
> >
> > **Solution.** CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 3 → C₃H₈, propane (a saturated hydrocarbon).

## What you should be able to do

- Recognise hydrocarbons and functional groups
- Name simple organic molecules (IUPAC)
- Explain carbon's versatility (catenation)

---

# Algorithmic Problem Solving

> [!intro] Problem-solving patterns and approaching problems under constraints.

## Patterns

Many problems fit patterns — two pointers, sliding window, greedy, dynamic programming. Recognising the pattern suggests an approach.

## Under constraints

Competitive and real problems limit time and memory. Choosing an algorithm whose complexity fits the constraints is the key skill.

```formula Key syntax & rules
Match the problem to a known pattern
Let input size guide the acceptable complexity
Get it correct first, then optimise
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** For n up to 10⁶, is an O(n²) solution acceptable?
> >
> > **Solution.** No — n² = 10¹² operations is far too slow. Aim for O(n) or O(n log n).

## What you should be able to do

- Recognise common patterns
- Approach constrained problems
- Balance correctness and efficiency

---

# Algorithms II

> [!intro] Divide and conquer, efficient sorting (merge/quick), and hashing.

## Divide and conquer

Split a problem, solve the parts, combine — the strategy behind merge sort and binary search. It often turns O(n²) into O(n log n).

## Hashing

A hash maps keys to array positions for near-instant lookup — how dictionaries and sets are fast. Understanding it explains their performance.

```formula Key syntax & rules
Divide and conquer: split, solve, combine
Merge/quick sort: O(n log n)
Hashing → ~O(1) average lookup
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Why is merge sort O(n log n)?
> >
> > **Solution.** It splits the list in half (log n levels of splitting) and does O(n) work merging at each level → n·log n.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply divide and conquer
- Explain merge and quick sort
- Use hashing for fast lookup

---

# Object-Oriented Programming (Python)

> [!intro] Classes, objects, encapsulation and inheritance — modelling with objects.

## Objects bundle data and behaviour

A class is a blueprint; objects are instances with their own data (attributes) and actions (methods). OOP models real-world entities in code.

## Inheritance and encapsulation

Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another; encapsulation keeps internal detail hidden behind a clean interface. Both manage complexity in large programs.

```formula Key syntax & rules
class = blueprint; object = instance
Methods take self as the first parameter
Inheritance reuses; encapsulation hides detail
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What is the difference between a class and an object?
> >
> > **Solution.** A class is the blueprint (e.g., Dog); an object is a specific instance made from it (e.g., my_dog = Dog()).

## What you should be able to do

- Define classes and create objects
- Use encapsulation
- Apply inheritance

cs.A1.recursion.summary: Thinking recursively, base cases, and recursion vs iteration.
cs.A1.recursion.notes:
# Recursion

> [!intro] Thinking recursively, base cases, and recursion vs iteration.

## A function that calls itself

Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a smaller version of itself, until a base case stops the recursion. It suits naturally nested problems (trees, factorials).

## Base case is essential

Without a base case, recursion never stops (stack overflow). Every recursion needs a shrinking input and a stopping condition.

```formula Key syntax & rules
Every recursion needs a base case
Each call moves toward the base case
No base case → stack overflow
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Trace factorial(3) with factorial(n)=n·factorial(n−1), base factorial(0)=1.
> >
> > **Solution.** 3·factorial(2) = 3·2·factorial(1) = 3·2·1·factorial(0) = 3·2·1·1 = 6.

## What you should be able to do

- Write recursive functions
- Identify base and recursive cases
- Compare recursion and iteration

---

# Testing

> [!intro] Writing tests and thinking about edge cases.

## Tests check behaviour

A test runs code with known input and checks the output. Automated tests catch bugs early and prevent regressions when you change code.

## Edge cases

Bugs hide at the edges: empty input, one element, maximum values, invalid input. Thinking about edges is where good testing lives.

```formula Key syntax & rules
Test normal, boundary and invalid inputs
A failing test pins down a bug
Re-run tests after every change (catch regressions)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What edge cases should you test for a function that averages a list?
> >
> > **Solution.** An empty list (avoid divide-by-zero), a single element, and negative numbers.

## What you should be able to do

- Write basic tests
- Identify edge cases
- Use tests to catch regressions

---

# Trees & Graphs

> [!intro] Representing and traversing trees and graphs (BFS/DFS).

## Nonlinear structures

Trees (hierarchies) and graphs (networks) model relationships lists cannot — file systems, maps, social networks. Nodes connect via edges.

## Traversal

BFS explores level by level (using a queue); DFS goes deep first (using a stack/recursion). The right traversal depends on the problem.

```formula Key syntax & rules
BFS uses a queue (level by level)
DFS uses a stack/recursion (deep first)
Mark visited nodes to avoid cycles
Tree = acyclic graph
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** To find the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph, BFS or DFS?
> >
> > **Solution.** BFS — it explores level by level, so it reaches a node by the fewest edges first.

## What you should be able to do

- Represent trees and graphs
- Traverse with BFS and DFS
- Choose a traversal for a task

---

cs.A2.databases-intro.notes:
# Databases Intro

> [!intro] Relational modelling and basic SQL.

## Relational model

A database stores data in tables (rows and columns) with keys linking related tables. This structures data far better than files for many applications.

## SQL

SQL queries data: SELECT to read, WHERE to filter, JOIN to combine tables. It is a declarative language — you say what you want, not how to get it.

```formula Key syntax & rules
Data in tables (rows, columns) linked by keys
SELECT reads, WHERE filters, JOIN combines
SQL is declarative (what, not how)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Write SQL to get names of users older than 18.
> >
> > **Solution.** SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 18; — SELECT chooses the column, WHERE filters the rows.

## What you should be able to do

- Model data in tables
- Write basic SQL queries
- Understand keys and relationships

---

# Booleans & Conditionals

> [!intro] if/elif/else and boolean logic — making programs decide.

## Making decisions

Conditionals run different code depending on whether a condition is True or False. if/elif/else lets a program choose a path — the basis of all logic.

## Boolean logic

Conditions combine with and, or, not. Understanding truth values (from maths logic) lets you express complex decisions correctly.

```formula Key syntax & rules
== compares; = assigns
if / elif / else chooses a branch
and / or / not combine conditions
Indentation defines the block
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** What prints? x = 7; print("big" if x > 5 else "small")
> >
> > **Solution.** big — since 7 > 5 is True, the expression yields "big".

## What you should be able to do

- Use if/elif/else
- Combine conditions with and/or/not
- Trace which branch runs

# Computational Thinking

> [!intro] Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms — thinking before coding.

## Four pillars

Computational thinking is decomposition (break it down), pattern recognition (spot repetition), abstraction (ignore irrelevant detail), and algorithms (precise step-by-step recipes).

## Algorithms are recipes

An algorithm is an unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem. Getting the thinking right on paper makes the coding straightforward.

```formula Key syntax & rules
Decomposition: break a big problem into parts
Pattern recognition → reuse solutions
Abstraction: ignore irrelevant detail
Algorithm: precise, unambiguous steps
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Decompose "make tea" into an algorithm (3+ steps).
> >
> > **Solution.** 1) Boil water. 2) Put a tea bag in a cup. 3) Pour water in. 4) Wait 3 min, remove bag. Each step is precise and ordered.

## What you should be able to do

- Break problems into parts (decomposition)
- Spot patterns and generalise
- Write algorithms as precise steps

---
