math.I1.trigonometry-i.notes:
# Trigonometry I

> [!intro] **Trigonometry exists because of similarity.** All right triangles with the same acute angle are similar, so their side *ratios* depend only on that angle — never on size. Those fixed ratios get names (sine, cosine, tangent), and suddenly you can find distances you cannot measure: the height of a tower, the width of a river, the resolved components of a force in physics.

## 1. Why the ratios are well-defined

Take any right triangle with an acute angle $\theta$. Any other right triangle with the same $\theta$ has the same three angles, so by **AA** the two are similar (F2 Geometry II), and corresponding sides are in proportion.

Therefore the ratio $\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ is **the same for every** right triangle containing that angle. It depends on $\theta$ alone — so it deserves a name, and it is called $\sin\theta$.

Relative to the chosen angle $\theta$:

- **Opposite** — the side facing $\theta$.
- **Adjacent** — the side touching $\theta$ that is not the hypotenuse.
- **Hypotenuse** — opposite the right angle; always the longest, and never changes role.

$$\sin\theta = \frac{O}{H}, \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{A}{H}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{O}{A}$$

remembered as **SOH-CAH-TOA**.

**Opposite and adjacent swap when you change reference angle** — this is the single biggest source of error. The hypotenuse is fixed by the right angle, but the other two labels depend entirely on which acute angle you are working from. Label the triangle *after* choosing $\theta$, every time.

Two immediate consequences: since $O < H$ and $A < H$, both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are **always less than 1** for an acute angle. An answer of $\sin\theta = 1.4$ is impossible — a reliable error detector. $\tan\theta$, however, has no such bound.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Right triangle labelled opposite adjacent hypotenuse" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <polygon points="70,140 320,140 320,40" fill="none" stroke="#6ee7a8" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <rect x="303" y="123" width="17" height="17" fill="none" stroke="#9aa8c4" stroke-width="2"/>
  <path d="M110 140 A 40 40 0 0 0 100 118" fill="none" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="112" y="128" font-size="13" fill="#6366f1">θ</text>
  <text x="180" y="158" font-size="12" fill="#9aa8c4">adjacent</text>
  <text x="330" y="95" font-size="12" fill="#9aa8c4">opposite</text>
  <text x="160" y="80" font-size="12" fill="#9aa8c4">hypotenuse</text>
  <text x="70" y="24" font-size="11" fill="#e6ecff">labels depend on which angle is θ</text>
</svg>
```

## 2. Using the ratios: find a side, find an angle

**To find a side**, pick the ratio containing the side you want and the side you know.

A ladder makes $60°$ with the ground and reaches 4 m up a wall. How long is the ladder? Here the 4 m is *opposite* the $60°$ and the ladder is the *hypotenuse*, so use sine:

$$\sin 60° = \frac{4}{L} \Rightarrow L = \frac{4}{\sin 60°} \approx \frac{4}{0.866} \approx 4.6 \text{ m}$$

**To find an angle**, use the inverse functions $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$ (also written arcsin, etc.). If the opposite is 3 and the adjacent 4:

$$\tan\theta = \tfrac34 \Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.9°$$

Two mechanical cautions that cause more lost marks than any concept here:

- **$\sin^{-1}$ is not $\dfrac{1}{\sin}$.** It is the inverse *function* — "which angle has this ratio?" The reciprocal $\tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ is a different thing entirely (called cosec).
- **Check the calculator is in degrees.** A calculator in radian mode gives confidently wrong answers with no warning. Verify by computing $\sin 30°$: it must be exactly 0.5.

**Choosing which ratio to use:** label the three sides relative to your angle, mark which two are involved (one known, one wanted), and the pair names the ratio. Only one of SOH, CAH, TOA will fit.

> [!example] **Angle of elevation**
>
> **Problem.** From 50 m away, the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is 32°. How tall is the tower?
>
> **Solution.** The 50 m is *adjacent* to the angle and the height is *opposite*, so use tangent: $\tan 32° = \dfrac{h}{50}$, giving $h = 50\tan 32° \approx 50 \times 0.625 \approx 31.2$ m.
>
> *Angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal; angle of depression is measured down from it — and the two are equal between the same pair of points (alternate angles).*

## 3. The exact values, and where they come from

Three angles have exact ratios you should know without a calculator, and they come from two simple triangles.

**The $45°$ triangle:** take a unit square and cut along the diagonal. Both legs are 1 and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt2$, so $\sin45° = \cos45° = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\tan45° = 1$.

**The $30°$–$60°$ triangle:** take an equilateral triangle of side 2 and drop a perpendicular. It splits into two right triangles with hypotenuse 2, short side 1 and (by Pythagoras) long side $\sqrt3$.

| $\theta$ | $\sin$ | $\cos$ | $\tan$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0°$ | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| $30°$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ |
| $45°$ | $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | 1 |
| $60°$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\sqrt3$ |
| $90°$ | 1 | 0 | undefined |

Read the pattern rather than memorising 15 numbers: **sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows; cosine decreases from 1 to 0**; and the $30°$ and $60°$ values are each other's swapped. That reflects the identity $\sin\theta = \cos(90°-\theta)$ — the two acute angles in a right triangle are complementary, and one's opposite is the other's adjacent.

$\tan 90°$ is undefined because the adjacent side shrinks to zero, and division by zero is undefined — the same reason a vertical line has no gradient.

```formula Key formulas
sin θ = O/H,  cos θ = A/H,  tan θ = O/A  (SOH-CAH-TOA)
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1  (Pythagoras, in ratio form)
sin θ = cos(90° − θ)
For acute θ: 0 < sin θ < 1 and 0 < cos θ < 1
```

## 4. The unit circle and the first identity

Place a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 inside a circle of radius 1, with $\theta$ at the origin. Then the horizontal leg is $\cos\theta$ and the vertical leg is $\sin\theta$ — so the point on the circle is exactly $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$.

Applying Pythagoras to that triangle gives the most important identity in trigonometry:

$$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$$

(The notation $\sin^2\theta$ means $(\sin\theta)^2$, not $\sin(\theta^2)$.) This is not a new fact — it *is* Pythagoras, written with ratios instead of lengths.

It is immediately useful: given $\sin\theta = \tfrac35$ for an acute angle, $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25}$, so $\cos\theta = \tfrac45$, and then $\tan\theta = \tfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tfrac34$. One ratio determines the other two.

The unit circle also explains what happens **beyond $90°$**, where "opposite over hypotenuse" no longer makes sense: the coordinates keep going, so $\sin$ and $\cos$ are defined for any angle, taking negative values in the appropriate quadrants. That extension — and the wave shape it produces — is the subject of Trigonometry II, and it is why sine describes oscillations in physics.

> [!example] **One ratio gives the rest**
>
> **Problem.** For an acute angle, $\sin\theta = \tfrac35$. Find $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$.
>
> **Solution.** From $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$: $\cos^2\theta = 1-\tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25}$, so $\cos\theta = \tfrac45$ (positive, since $\theta$ is acute). Then $\tan\theta = \tfrac{3/5}{4/5} = \tfrac34$.
>
> *This is the 3-4-5 triangle — recognising Pythagorean triples makes trigonometry questions instant.*

```formula Key formulas
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = O/H, cos = A/H, tan = O/A
Inverse functions sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ find the ANGLE (not a reciprocal)
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1;  tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
Exact: sin30 = ½, cos60 = ½, sin45 = cos45 = 1/√2, tan45 = 1, tan60 = √3
sin θ = cos(90° − θ)
```

## What you should be able to do

- Use sin, cos and tan in right triangles
- Solve for unknown sides and angles
- Understand the unit-circle picture

## Summary — the mental toolkit

1. The ratios are well-defined because all right triangles with a given acute angle are similar.
2. Opposite and adjacent depend on the chosen angle; only the hypotenuse is fixed.
3. For acute angles sin and cos are always below 1 — a built-in error check.
4. Pick the ratio from the two sides involved: one known, one wanted.
5. Inverse functions find angles; sin⁻¹ is not 1/sin, and the calculator must be in degrees.
6. The 45° and 30°–60° triangles generate all the exact values worth memorising.
7. sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is Pythagoras in ratio form, and one ratio determines the other two.

---

math.I1.trigonometry-i.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Trigonometry I

> Every learner hits these. Read the *why* — that is what stops the mistake coming back.

- **Mislabelling opposite and adjacent** after switching reference angle. **Fix:** choose θ first, then label all three sides relative to it. Only the hypotenuse keeps its role.

- **Treating sin⁻¹ as 1/sin.** **Fix:** sin⁻¹ answers "which angle gives this ratio?" The reciprocal 1/sin θ is cosec θ, a different quantity.

- **Leaving the calculator in radian mode.** Answers are wrong with no warning. **Fix:** test sin 30° — it must be exactly 0.5.

- **Accepting sin θ > 1.** **Fix:** impossible for any angle, since the opposite side cannot exceed the hypotenuse. Recheck which side you called the hypotenuse.

- **Using the ratios in a non-right triangle.** SOH-CAH-TOA requires a right angle. **Fix:** either drop a perpendicular to create one, or wait for the sine and cosine rules in Trigonometry II.

- **Multiplying when you should divide** when the unknown is in the denominator. From sin 60° = 4/L, writing L = 4 sin 60°. **Fix:** rearranging gives L = 4 ÷ sin 60°; check that the hypotenuse came out as the longest side.

- **Reading sin²θ as sin(θ²).** **Fix:** sin²θ means (sin θ)², the ratio squared.

- **Rounding intermediate values** and carrying the error forward. **Fix:** keep full precision in the calculator until the final answer, then round once.
math.I1.trigonometry-i.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Trigonometry I

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic — and when each one applies.

- **Sketch and label the triangle before touching a calculator.** Most trigonometry errors are labelling errors, not arithmetic ones.

- **Check plausibility with the size rule:** the side opposite the larger angle is longer, and the hypotenuse is longest of all.

- **Reconstruct the exact values from the two special triangles** (unit square cut diagonally; equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half) rather than memorising a table you might misremember.

- **Use sin θ = cos(90° − θ)** to halve what you need to recall.

- **Spot Pythagorean triples in trig questions** — 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 turn a calculation into instant recall.

- **When the unknown is in the denominator, take reciprocals of both sides** rather than cross-multiplying under pressure.

- **Verify a found angle by substituting back** into the original ratio.

math.I2.combinatorics-probability-ii.notes:
# Combinatorics & Probability II

> [!intro] Counting principles, permutations and combinations, and conditional probability.

## Counting systematically

The multiplication principle counts multi-step choices; permutations count ordered arrangements, combinations count unordered selections. Choosing the right one is the whole skill.

## Conditional probability

P(A|B) is the probability of A given B has happened. It corrects naive counting when events depend on one another — the heart of genetics and risk.

```formula Key formulas
nPr = n!/(n−r)!  (order matters)
nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!)  (order does not)
P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** How many ways to choose a committee of 3 from 6 people?
> >
> > **Solution.** 6C3 = 6!/(3!·3!) = 720/(6·6) = 20 ways.

## What you should be able to do

- Count with permutations and combinations
- Use the multiplication principle
- Compute conditional probability

---

math.I2.derivatives-intuition.notes:
# Calculus Intuition: Derivatives

> [!intro] Rate of change made exact — the derivative as the slope of a curve, taught alongside kinematics.

## Instantaneous rate

The derivative measures how fast a quantity changes at an instant — the slope of the tangent to its graph. It makes the "slope = rate" idea from lines exact for curves.

## Power rule

For f(x) = xⁿ, the derivative is n·x^(n−1). This single rule differentiates polynomials and connects directly to velocity being the derivative of position.

```formula Key formulas
d/dx (xⁿ) = n·x^(n−1)
d/dx (constant) = 0
f'(x) = slope of the tangent = instantaneous rate
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Differentiate f(x) = x³ − 4x and find the slope at x = 2.
> >
> > **Solution.** f'(x) = 3x² − 4. At x = 2: 3(4) − 4 = 8. The tangent slope at x = 2 is 8.

## What you should be able to do

- Interpret the derivative as an instantaneous rate
- Differentiate simple powers
- Connect derivative to slope of a tangent

---

math.I2.exponentials-logarithms.notes:
# Exponentials & Logarithms

> [!intro] Exponential growth and decay, logarithms as the inverse, and their laws — used across chemistry, biology and CS.

## Exponential change

Exponential functions grow or decay by a constant factor per step — populations, radioactive decay, compound interest. The rate of change is proportional to the current amount.

## Logarithms invert exponentials

log_b(x) answers "what power of b gives x?". Log laws (log(ab)=log a+log b) turn multiplication into addition — the reason logs simplify pH, decibels and algorithmic complexity.

```formula Key formulas
log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y
log_b(xⁿ) = n log_b x
b^x = y ⇔ log_b y = x
Growth: N = N₀ · e^(kt)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Solve 2^x = 32.
> >
> > **Solution.** Take logs: x = log₂ 32 = 5, since 2⁵ = 32.

## What you should be able to do

- Work with exponential functions
- Use logarithms and their laws
- Model growth and decay

---

math.I2.functions.notes:
# Functions as Objects

> [!intro] Function notation, domain and range, composition, inverses and transformations of graphs.

## A function is a machine

A function f takes an input and returns exactly one output, written f(x). Domain is the allowed inputs, range the possible outputs. Thinking of functions as objects you can combine is a big conceptual step.

## Composition and inverses

Composition f(g(x)) feeds one function's output into another. The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f. Graph transformations (shifts, stretches, reflections) change a function predictably.

```formula Key formulas
f: one input → exactly one output
Composition: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))
Inverse: swap x and y, solve for y
Vertical-line test checks if a graph is a function
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find f(g(3)).
> >
> > **Solution.** g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.

## What you should be able to do

- Use function notation and find domain/range
- Compose and invert functions
- Transform graphs (shift, stretch, reflect)

---

math.I2.integrals-intuition.notes:
# Calculus Intuition: Integrals

> [!intro] Accumulation and area under a curve — the reverse of differentiation.

## Area as accumulation

The integral adds up infinitely many thin slices to give the area under a curve — which represents total accumulated quantity (e.g., distance from a velocity graph).

## The reverse of the derivative

Integration undoes differentiation: ∫xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C. This Fundamental Theorem links the two halves of calculus.

```formula Key formulas
∫ xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C  (n ≠ −1)
Definite integral = signed area under the curve
Integration undoes differentiation
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 3 of 2x dx.
> >
> > **Solution.** ∫ 2x dx = x². Evaluate 0→3: 3² − 0² = 9. (This is the area of the triangle under y = 2x.)

## What you should be able to do

- Interpret an integral as accumulated area
- Integrate simple powers
- Relate integration and differentiation

---

math.I2.trigonometry-ii.notes:
# Trigonometry II

> [!intro] Identities, trigonometric equations, and the sine and cosine rules for any triangle.

## Identities

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and the addition formulas let you rewrite and simplify trig expressions. Identities are the algebra of trigonometry.

## Rules for any triangle

The sine rule (a/sin A = b/sin B) and cosine rule (c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C) extend trig to non-right triangles — vital in physics and surveying.

```formula Key formulas
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
Cosine rule: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A triangle has sides a=5, b=7 with included angle C=60°. Find c.
> >
> > **Solution.** c² = 5² + 7² − 2·5·7·cos60° = 25 + 49 − 70(0.5) = 74 − 35 = 39 → c = √39 ≈ 6.24.

## What you should be able to do

- Use key trig identities
- Solve trigonometric equations
- Apply the sine and cosine rules

---

physics.A1.electrostatics.notes:
# Electrostatics

> [!intro] Electric charge, fields, potential and capacitance, using calculus and vectors.

## Charge and field

Like charges repel, unlike attract, with force F = kq₁q₂/r² (an inverse-square law like gravity). The electric field E = F/q describes force per unit charge.

## Potential and capacitance

Electric potential is energy per unit charge; the field points from high to low potential. Capacitance measures stored charge per volt.

```formula Key formulas
Coulomb: F = kq₁q₂/r²
Field E = F/q
Field points high → low potential
Capacitance C = Q/V
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Two charges are separated, then the distance is halved. How does the force change?
> >
> > **Solution.** F ∝ 1/r². Halving r gives F × (1/(1/2)²) = ×4 the original force.

## What you should be able to do

- Use Coulomb's law and electric fields
- Relate field and potential
- Analyse capacitance

---

physics.A1.fluids-advanced.notes:
# Fluids at A-Level

> [!intro] Fluid pressure, viscosity and an introduction to Bernoulli's principle.

## Static and moving fluids

Pressure in a static fluid rises with depth (P = ρgh). In steady flow, the continuity equation says a narrower pipe means faster flow.

## Bernoulli

Where a fluid moves faster, its pressure drops. This explains lift, spray guns and curveballs — energy conservation for flowing fluids.

```formula Key formulas
Static pressure P = ρgh
Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂
Bernoulli: faster flow ↔ lower pressure
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Water flows through a pipe that narrows from area 4 cm² to 1 cm². If inlet speed is 2 m/s, find the outlet speed.
> >
> > **Solution.** A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → 4×2 = 1×v₂ → v₂ = 8 m/s.

## What you should be able to do

- Analyse pressure in static and moving fluids
- Explain viscosity and flow
- Apply Bernoulli qualitatively

---

physics.A1.gravitation-field.notes:
# Gravitation (Field Treatment)

> [!intro] Gravitational fields, potential and energy, and orbital mechanics at depth.

## Fields and potential

A gravitational field g = F/m describes the force per unit mass at each point. Gravitational potential and PE track the energy of a mass in the field.

## Orbital energy

An orbit's total energy (kinetic + potential) determines its shape and whether it is bound. Escape velocity is the speed needed to reach zero total energy.

```formula Key formulas
Field g = GM/r²
Escape velocity v = √(2GM/r)
Bound orbit → negative total energy
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** At what multiple of Earth’s radius does g fall to 1/4 of its surface value?
> >
> > **Solution.** g ∝ 1/r². g/4 when r² = 4 → r = 2R. So at twice Earth’s radius from the centre.

## What you should be able to do

- Use gravitational field strength and potential
- Compute gravitational PE
- Analyse orbits energetically

---

physics.A1.mechanics-rigor.notes:
# Mechanics at Full Rigor

> [!intro] Dynamics with calculus, the work-energy theorem, and rotational motion of rigid bodies.

## Work-energy theorem

The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy. With calculus, this handles varying forces that SUVAT cannot.

## Rotation

Rotating bodies have angular versions of every linear quantity: torque (force), moment of inertia (mass), angular momentum. Newton's laws reappear in rotational form.

```formula Key formulas
Work–energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE
Torque τ = r × F = rF sin θ
Angular momentum conserved with no external torque
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A 3 kg object speeds up from 2 to 5 m/s. Find the net work done.
> >
> > **Solution.** W = ΔKE = ½m(v² − u²) = ½·3·(25 − 4) = ½·3·21 = 31.5 J.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the work-energy theorem
- Analyse rotational dynamics
- Use torque and moment of inertia

---

physics.A1.thermodynamics.notes:
# Thermodynamics

> [!intro] The laws of thermodynamics, heat engines and entropy — sharing a spine with chemistry.

## First and second laws

The first law is energy conservation: ΔU = Q − W. The second says entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases — setting a direction for time and limits on engines.

## Heat engines

Engines convert heat to work but never fully; the second law caps their efficiency. This links directly to chemistry's energetics.

```formula Key formulas
First law: ΔU = Q − W
Second law: entropy of isolated system never decreases
No engine is 100% efficient (Carnot limit)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Find the change in internal energy.
> >
> > **Solution.** ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = 300 J.

## What you should be able to do

- State the laws of thermodynamics
- Analyse heat engines and efficiency
- Explain entropy intuitively

---

# Current Electricity & Circuits (Full Rigor)

> [!intro] DC circuits at depth: networks, power dissipation, and measurement.

## Networks and power

Combining series and parallel rules solves any resistor network; Kirchhoff's laws handle the rest. Power dissipated is P = I²R = VI.

## Measurement

Ammeters (low resistance, in series) and voltmeters (high resistance, in parallel) measure without disturbing the circuit much — a design consequence of the circuit laws.

```formula Key formulas
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Ammeter in series (low R), voltmeter in parallel (high R)
Reduce networks in series/parallel stages
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A 3 Ω resistor carries 2 A. Find the power dissipated.
> >
> > **Solution.** P = I²R = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12 W.

## What you should be able to do

- Analyse complex resistor networks
- Compute electrical power
- Use measurement circuits

physics.A2.electromagnetic-induction.notes:
# Magnetic Effects & Electromagnetic Induction

> [!intro] Magnetic forces, Faraday's and Lenz's laws, and AC circuits — using differential equations.

## Induction

A changing magnetic flux induces an EMF (Faraday); the induced current opposes the change (Lenz). This is how generators and transformers work.

## AC circuits

Alternating current varies sinusoidally; inductors and capacitors respond to its rate of change, described naturally by differential equations.

```formula Key formulas
Faraday: EMF = −dΦ/dt (Φ = magnetic flux)
Lenz: induced current opposes the change
Only changing flux induces an EMF
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Magnetic flux through a coil changes from 0.2 to 0.6 Wb in 0.1 s. Find the magnitude of the induced EMF.
> >
> > **Solution.** EMF = ΔΦ/Δt = (0.6 − 0.2)/0.1 = 0.4/0.1 = 4 V.

## What you should be able to do

- Compute magnetic force on currents/charges
- Apply Faraday's and Lenz's laws
- Analyse simple AC circuits

---

physics.A2.experimental-physics.notes:
# Experimental Physics Portfolio

> [!intro] Error analysis, real measurement and scientific write-ups — the capstone lab strand.

## Uncertainty is unavoidable

Every measurement has an uncertainty; reporting it honestly is part of the result. Uncertainties combine by defined rules when quantities are added or multiplied.

## From data to conclusion

Good experiments control variables, repeat for reliability, and use graphs (often straight-line fits) to extract results. The write-up must let another person reproduce it.

```formula Key formulas
Repeat and average to reduce random error
Precision = repeatability; accuracy = closeness to true
Adding quantities: add absolute uncertainties
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Readings 4.9, 5.1, 5.0 s are precise but the true value is 6.0 s. Precise or accurate?
> >
> > **Solution.** They agree closely (precise) but are far from 6.0 s (not accurate) — likely a systematic error.

## What you should be able to do

- Estimate and propagate uncertainty
- Design and record experiments
- Write clear lab reports

---

physics.A2.modern-physics.notes:
# Modern Physics

> [!intro] The photoelectric effect, atomic models, nuclei and radioactivity, and semiconductor basics.

## Quantum beginnings

The photoelectric effect shows light comes in packets (photons) with energy E = hf. This launched quantum physics and explained atomic spectra.

## Nuclei and radioactivity

Unstable nuclei decay (alpha, beta, gamma), each decay halving the sample over one half-life. Mass converts to energy via E = mc².

```formula Key formulas
Photon energy E = hf
Mass–energy E = mc²
After n half-lives, fraction remaining = (1/2)ⁿ
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A radioactive sample has a half-life of 5 years. What fraction remains after 15 years?
> >
> > **Solution.** 15/5 = 3 half-lives → (1/2)³ = 1/8 = 0.125 remains.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain the photoelectric effect
- Describe atomic and nuclear models
- Understand radioactivity and half-life

---

physics.A2.optics-advanced.notes:
# Optics at Full Rigor

> [!intro] Wave optics: interference, diffraction and the wave nature of light.

## Wave optics

Light's wave nature shows up as interference (double-slit fringes) and diffraction (spreading around edges). Path difference of a whole wavelength gives bright fringes.

## Evidence for waves

These effects cannot be explained by rays alone — they were the historic proof that light is a wave, later refined by quantum theory.

```formula Key formulas
Bright fringe: path difference = nλ
Double slit fringe spacing y = λD/d
Narrow slit ⇒ more diffraction
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** In a double slit, slit spacing d = 0.5 mm, screen distance D = 2 m, λ = 500 nm. Find the fringe spacing.
> >
> > **Solution.** y = λD/d = (500×10⁻⁹ × 2)/(0.5×10⁻³) = (10⁻⁶)/(0.5×10⁻³) = 2×10⁻³ m = 2 mm.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain interference and diffraction
- Analyse the double-slit experiment
- Relate path difference to fringes

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. The three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth; modules are deepened over time._

outcomes: Relate work done to energy change
physics.F1.energy-i.notes:
# Energy I

> [!intro] Work, kinetic and potential energy, and conservation of energy as an accounting principle.

## Work transfers energy

Work = force × distance in the direction of the force. Doing work on an object changes its energy — the work-energy link.

## Conservation as accounting

Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed. Total energy before = total after; tracking KE (½mv²) and PE (mgh) like a ledger solves many problems without forces.

```formula Key formulas
Work W = F·d (force along motion)
Kinetic energy KE = ½mv²
Potential energy PE = mgh
Energy is conserved (transforms, not lost)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A 2 kg ball is dropped from 5 m. Find its speed just before impact (g = 10).
> >
> > **Solution.** PE → KE: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh) = √(2·10·5) = √100 = 10 m/s.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate work, KE and PE
- Apply conservation of energy
- Relate work done to energy change

---

physics.F1.force-newtons-laws.notes:
# Force & Newton's Laws (Introductory)

> [!intro] Forces as pushes and pulls, and Newton's three laws applied quantitatively in one dimension.

## The three laws

A body stays at rest or constant velocity unless a net force acts (1st law); force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma (2nd law); every force has an equal and opposite reaction (3rd law).

## Net force decides motion

It is the net (resultant) force that causes acceleration. Balanced forces mean no acceleration — not necessarily no motion.

```formula Key formulas
F = ma
Net force = 0 ⇒ constant velocity (1st law)
Action = −Reaction (3rd law, on different bodies)
Weight W = mg
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A 4 kg block accelerates at 2.5 m/s². Find the net force.
> >
> > **Solution.** F = ma = 4 × 2.5 = 10 N.

## What you should be able to do

- State and apply Newton's three laws
- Use F = ma in 1-D
- Identify action-reaction pairs

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. The three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth; modules are deepened over time._

physics.F1.measurement-units-estimation.notes:
# Measurement, Units & Estimation

> [!intro] SI units, unit conversion as ratio reasoning, significant figures and Fermi estimation.

## Measurement needs units

A number without a unit is meaningless in physics. SI units (metre, kilogram, second) form a consistent system, and converting between units is just scaling a ratio.

## Significant figures and estimation

Significant figures communicate precision honestly. Fermi estimation — breaking a hard quantity into rough factors — gives a defensible ballpark and checks detailed answers.

```formula Key formulas
1 km = 1000 m, 1 h = 3600 s
m/s → km/h: ×3.6
Estimate by rounding each factor to 1 s.f.
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Convert 15 m/s to km/h.
> >
> > **Solution.** 15 × 3.6 = 54 km/h.

## What you should be able to do

- Use SI units and convert between them
- Apply significant figures
- Make order-of-magnitude estimates

---

physics.F1.motion.title: Motion: Speed, Velocity & Acceleration
physics.F1.motion.summary: Speed is a rate — a ratio of distance to time — so this topic reuses ratio/proportion instead of re-teaching it, then extends to velocity, acceleration, and motion graphs.

physics.F1.motion.notes:
# Motion: Speed, Velocity & Acceleration

> **You already know most of this.** In *Math F1 — Ratio, Proportion & Percentage* you learned that a **rate is a ratio of unlike quantities**. Speed is exactly that: a ratio of distance to time. We are **not** going to re-teach "divide distance by time" as if it were new — we're going to *apply* the rate idea you already own to the physical world, then push it further into velocity, acceleration, and graphs. This reuse is deliberate: it's how the program covers physics in less time without losing anything.

## 1. Speed is a rate (the reuse)

$$ \text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time taken}} $$

That fraction is a **rate** — a ratio of unlike quantities (metres and seconds), carrying its units, exactly as you met with price (₹/kg) and density (mass/volume). Everything you learned about rates transfers:
- **Scaling to convert units** is just simplifying a ratio: $5\text{ m/s} \times \frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ h}} \times \frac{1\text{ km}}{1000\text{ m}} = 18\text{ km/h}$. (Multiply by 3.6 to go m/s → km/h; divide by 3.6 to go back.)
- **Average speed is total-over-total**, never the plain average of two speeds — the *exact* trap you met in the ratio quiz.

$$ \text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}. $$

> **Worked example.** A car does 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 60 km/h. Average speed? Time = 60/30 + 60/60 = 2 + 1 = 3 h; total distance 120 km; average = 120/3 = **40 km/h** — not 45. Same reasoning as mixing quantities in a ratio.

## 2. Distance vs displacement, speed vs velocity (scalar vs vector)

Physics adds one idea ratios didn't need: **direction**.

- **Distance** — how much ground you covered (a **scalar**, no direction). Always ≥ 0.
- **Displacement** — the straight-line change in position, *with direction* (a **vector**). Can be zero even after a long walk if you return to start.
- **Speed** = distance / time (scalar). **Velocity** = displacement / time (vector — it has direction).

> Walk 3 km east then 3 km west in 2 hours: distance = 6 km, speed = 3 km/h; displacement = 0, velocity = 0. The numbers differ because one tracks *path length*, the other tracks *net change in position*.

This scalar/vector distinction is the seed of the full vector treatment you'll meet in **Physics I1** — planted here so it's familiar, not formal yet.

## 3. Acceleration is *also* a rate — of velocity this time

The rate idea now stacks on itself. Acceleration is the **rate of change of velocity**:

$$ a = \frac{\text{change in velocity}}{\text{time taken}} = \frac{v - u}{t}, $$

where $u$ = initial velocity, $v$ = final velocity. Units: $\frac{\text{m/s}}{\text{s}} = \text{m/s}^2$.

- **Positive** acceleration → speeding up (in the chosen positive direction).
- **Negative** acceleration (deceleration/retardation) → slowing down.
- Acceleration is a vector: a car turning a corner at constant *speed* is still accelerating, because its velocity's *direction* is changing.

> **Worked example.** A bike goes from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. $a = (20 - 0)/5 = 4\text{ m/s}^2$. Each second it gains 4 m/s.

## 4. Motion graphs — where slope and area tell the story

Graphs turn motion into pictures. This reuses **Data & graphs (Math F1.7)** — reading slopes and areas.

### Distance–time (d–t) graph
- **Slope = speed.** Steeper line → faster. Horizontal line → at rest (distance not changing).
- A straight line → constant speed; a curve → changing speed.

### Velocity–time (v–t) graph — the workhorse
- **Slope = acceleration.** (Rise in velocity over run in time — a rate again.)
- **Area under the line = distance travelled.** A horizontal line (constant velocity) gives a rectangle: area = v × t = distance. A sloped line gives a triangle/trapezium.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" aria-label="Velocity-time graph: slope is acceleration, area is distance" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <line x1="40" y1="150" x2="280" y2="150" stroke="#6b7a99"/>
  <line x1="40" y1="150" x2="40" y2="20" stroke="#6b7a99"/>
  <text x="150" y="172" font-size="11" fill="#9aa8c4" text-anchor="middle">time →</text>
  <text x="14" y="90" font-size="11" fill="#9aa8c4" transform="rotate(-90 14 90)" text-anchor="middle">velocity →</text>
  <polygon points="40,150 240,60 240,150" fill="rgba(99,102,241,0.25)"/>
  <line x1="40" y1="150" x2="240" y2="60" stroke="#8fa0ff" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text x="150" y="135" font-size="11" fill="#a8c0ff" text-anchor="middle">area = distance</text>
  <text x="205" y="95" font-size="11" fill="#6ee7a8" transform="rotate(-24 205 95)">slope = a</text>
</svg>
```

> This "slope is the rate, area is the accumulation" pattern is exactly what becomes **derivatives and integrals** in Intermediate. You are seeing calculus in picture form two years before you formalise it — another deliberate reuse.

## 5. The equations of uniformly accelerated motion

When acceleration is **constant**, three equations follow directly from the definitions above (no new physics — just algebra applied to "slope = a" and "area = distance"):

$$ v = u + at \qquad s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 \qquad v^2 = u^2 + 2as $$

where $s$ = displacement, $u$ = initial velocity, $v$ = final velocity, $a$ = acceleration, $t$ = time.

- The **first** is just the definition of acceleration rearranged.
- The **second** is the area under a v–t graph (rectangle $ut$ + triangle $\tfrac12 at^2$).
- The **third** is the first two combined to remove $t$ — useful when you don't know the time.

> **Worked example.** A car accelerates from 10 m/s at $2\text{ m/s}^2$ for 4 s.
> $v = 10 + 2\times4 = 18\text{ m/s}$.
> $s = 10\times4 + \tfrac12\times2\times4^2 = 40 + 16 = 56\text{ m}$.
> Check with the third equation: $v^2 = 10^2 + 2\times2\times56 = 100 + 224 = 324$, so $v = 18$. ✓ (Cross-checking with a second equation is a habit worth building.)

## 6. Free fall — one important special case
Near Earth's surface, objects fall with a constant acceleration $g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ (often approximated as 10 for quick estimates), ignoring air resistance. Every equation above applies with $a = g$. Drop a stone from rest: after 2 s, $v = gt = 9.8\times2 = 19.6\text{ m/s}$; distance $= \tfrac12 g t^2 = \tfrac12\times9.8\times4 = 19.6\text{ m}$.

## 7. Summary — what's new vs what's reused
| Reused from Math F1 | New in this topic |
|---|---|
| Rate = ratio of unlike quantities | Direction: scalar vs vector (distance/displacement, speed/velocity) |
| Average = total ÷ total | Acceleration as rate-of-change of velocity |
| Unit scaling (m/s ↔ km/h) | Motion graphs: slope = rate, area = distance |
| Reading slopes/areas of graphs | The three equations of uniform acceleration; free fall |

The compression is visible right here: about half this topic is *your ratio skills in a new costume*. Master motion and you've also rehearsed the rate thinking that chemistry (rates, concentration) and later calculus will demand.
physics.F1.motion.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Motion

### 1. Averaging two speeds directly
"30 km/h for half the trip and 60 km/h for the other half → average 45 km/h." **Wrong** when the halves are equal *distances*.
> **Fix:** average speed = total distance ÷ total time, *always*. For equal distances at 30 and 60, it's 40 km/h. Compute the two times and add them. (This is the same "average of rates" trap from the ratio topic.)

### 2. Confusing distance with displacement (and speed with velocity)
Reporting velocity as non-zero for a round trip that returns to the start.
> **Fix:** displacement is *net* change in position with direction; a round trip has zero displacement, hence zero average velocity, even though distance and average speed are not zero.

### 3. Thinking constant speed means zero acceleration — even around a curve
"The car's speedometer reads a steady 40, so acceleration is zero."
> **Fix:** velocity includes direction. Turning changes direction, so velocity changes, so there *is* acceleration even at constant speed. Zero acceleration requires constant speed **and** constant direction.

### 4. Mixing up the slope of a d–t graph with a v–t graph
Reading "area" off a distance–time graph, or "slope" as distance.
> **Fix:** on a **distance–time** graph, slope = speed (area means nothing). On a **velocity–time** graph, slope = acceleration and **area = distance**. Label which graph you're looking at before extracting anything.

### 5. Using the uniform-acceleration equations when acceleration isn't constant
Applying $v = u + at$ to a car whose acceleration is changing.
> **Fix:** $v=u+at$, $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$, $v^2=u^2+2as$ hold **only** for constant acceleration. If a graph is curved (a not constant), you can't use them over that stretch.

### 6. Unit inconsistency (mixing km/h and m/s in one equation)
Plugging a speed in km/h and a time in seconds into the same equation.
> **Fix:** convert everything to a single system first — usually SI (metres, seconds, m/s, m/s²). Remember ÷3.6 for km/h → m/s.

### 7. Sign errors with deceleration
Treating a slowing object's acceleration as positive, or forgetting the minus sign.
> **Fix:** choose a positive direction and stick to it. If the object slows, $a$ has the opposite sign to the velocity. In free fall taking "up" as positive, $a = -g$.

### 8. Forgetting the ½ in s = ut + ½at²
Writing $s = ut + at^2$.
> **Fix:** the ½ comes from the *triangle* area under the v–t graph. Picture the triangle and the ½ is unforgettable.

### 9. Assuming an object at rest has no acceleration
"It's momentarily stopped at the top of its throw, so a = 0 there."
> **Fix:** at the top of a vertical throw, velocity is zero *for an instant* but acceleration is still $g$ downward — that's exactly why it starts falling. Velocity = 0 ≠ acceleration = 0.

### 10. Reading the area under a v–t graph as speed instead of distance
> **Fix:** area = (velocity) × (time) = distance/displacement. The *height* is velocity; the *area* is how far it went.
physics.F1.motion.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Motion

### 1. The ×3.6 shortcut for m/s ↔ km/h
Multiply m/s by **3.6** to get km/h; divide by 3.6 to reverse.
> 25 m/s × 3.6 = 90 km/h. (Because 3600 s/h ÷ 1000 m/km = 3.6.) Never derive the whole ratio under time pressure — just remember 3.6.

### 2. List u, v, a, s, t before touching an equation
Kinematics problems are "given three of {u, v, a, s, t}, find another." Write the five symbols, fill in what's known, and pick the equation that contains your knowns + unknown:
- no $s$? → $v = u + at$
- no $v$? → $s = ut + \tfrac12at^2$
- no $t$? → $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$

This turns every problem into pattern-matching instead of guessing.

### 3. "Slope is the rate, area is the amount" — read graphs instantly
On any motion graph: the **slope** tells you the rate (speed on d–t, acceleration on v–t); the **area** under a v–t line tells you the distance. Two phrases handle every graph question.

### 4. Use the v–t graph to derive equations you forget
Forgot $s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2$? Draw the v–t trapezium: a rectangle of height $u$ (area $ut$) plus a triangle of height $at$ (area $\tfrac12 \cdot t \cdot at = \tfrac12 at^2$). Add them — there's your equation, reconstructed from a picture.

### 5. Average velocity for constant acceleration = (u+v)/2
When acceleration is constant, the average velocity is just the midpoint of start and end: $\bar v = \frac{u+v}{2}$. So $s = \frac{u+v}{2}\,t$ — often the fastest route when you know $u$, $v$, and $t$.

### 6. Free fall: use g ≈ 10 for a quick estimate, 9.8 for accuracy
For mental checks, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$ makes numbers clean (drop for 3 s → v ≈ 30 m/s). Switch to 9.8 for a final answer if precision is asked.

### 7. Symmetry of vertical throws
Throw something straight up: time up = time down, and it returns to your hand at the **same speed** it left (opposite direction). Use the symmetry to halve the work — find the time to the top, double it for total flight.

### 8. Cross-check with a second equation
After solving for $v$ with $v = u + at$, verify with $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. If they disagree, you slipped a sign or a unit. Two-equation confirmation catches most exam errors cheaply.

### 9. Sanity-bracket the answer
Before trusting a computed speed, ask "is this physically sane?" A dropped stone reaching 500 m/s after 2 s is impossible ($g\times2 ≈ 20$ m/s). Estimation guards against decimal slips — the same habit you built in the ratio topic.

### 10. Direction bookkeeping with signs
Pick + direction once, write every vector (u, v, a, s) with the correct sign, and let the algebra handle the rest. A negative answer for displacement just means "in the negative direction" — that's information, not an error.
physics.F1.motion.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Motion

## Core anchors

- **"Speed is a rate — it's the ratio topic in a lab coat."** Distance ÷ time, a ratio of unlike quantities.
- **"Average speed = total distance ÷ total time."** Never the plain average of two speeds.
- **"Acceleration is the rate of a rate."** How fast velocity changes.
- **"Slope is the rate; area is the amount."** The two-phrase key to every motion graph.

## Mnemonics

- **"3.6 goes up, 3.6 comes down."** ×3.6 for m/s → km/h, ÷3.6 for km/h → m/s.
- **SUVAT** — the five kinematics symbols: **s** (displacement), **u** (initial velocity), **v** (final velocity), **a** (acceleration), **t** (time). List them, fill three, find the fourth.
- **"Don't lose the half"** — $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. The ½ is the triangle under the v–t graph.
- **"Scalar = size, Vector = size + direction."** Distance/speed are scalars; displacement/velocity/acceleration are vectors.

## Visualization

- **The v–t graph is your calculator.** Any uniform-acceleration problem = a trapezium. Height = velocity, slope = acceleration, area = distance. Draw it and read off answers; you rarely need to *remember* the equations because the picture regenerates them.
- **The round-trip picture.** Walk out and back: the path (distance) is long, but the arrow from start to finish (displacement) is zero. Fixes the scalar/vector confusion permanently.
- **Top-of-the-throw freeze-frame.** At the peak, the ball is momentarily still (v = 0) but gravity is still pulling (a = g ≠ 0) — which is exactly why it drops. Cements "v = 0 does not mean a = 0."

## Spaced-repetition prompts
_(Resurfaced at 1 → 3 → 7 → 16 → 35 days.)_

1. Convert 90 km/h to m/s. (→ 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s)
2. A car goes 0 → 30 m/s in 6 s. Acceleration? (→ 5 m/s²)
3. On a velocity–time graph, what does the slope represent? The area? (→ acceleration; distance)
4. A stone dropped from rest falls for 3 s. Speed just before landing (g = 10)? (→ 30 m/s)
5. You run 400 m around a track back to the start in 80 s. Average speed? Average velocity? (→ 5 m/s; 0, since displacement is 0)
6. Which equation has no time in it? (→ v² = u² + 2as)
7. Why is a car rounding a bend at constant speed still accelerating? (→ direction of velocity changes)

## The one-line recall card
> **Speed is a rate (a ratio with units); velocity and displacement carry direction; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; on graphs slope = rate and area = distance; for constant a use SUVAT — and don't lose the ½.**

1.prompt: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is the average speed in m/s?
1.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s. Speed is a rate — a ratio of distance to time.

1.prompt: Which quantity has a direction (is a vector)?
1.explanation: Velocity is displacement per time and carries direction (a vector). Distance, speed and time are scalars.

1.prompt: A car's velocity changes from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
1.explanation: a = (v − u)/t = (20 − 0)/4 = 5 m/s². Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

1.prompt: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
1.explanation: Divide by 3.6: 72 ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s. Unit conversion is ratio scaling.

1.prompt: On a distance–time graph, a horizontal (flat) line means the object is:
1.explanation: Flat line = distance not changing = at rest. The slope (which is zero here) equals the speed.

1.prompt: On a velocity–time graph, the slope of the line represents:
1.explanation: Slope of a v–t graph = change in velocity ÷ time = acceleration. (The AREA under it would be the distance.)

2.prompt: A car starts at 8 m/s and accelerates at 3 m/s² for 5 s. What is its final velocity in m/s?
A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 6 s. How far does it travel, in metres?
2.explanation: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½×2×6² = ½×2×36 = 36 m. Don't lose the ½.

2.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 3 s. Using g = 10 m/s², what is its speed just before landing, in m/s?
2.explanation: v = u + gt = 0 + 10×3 = 30 m/s. Free fall uses the same equations with a = g.

2.prompt: A cyclist rides 3 km east then 3 km west, taking 30 minutes total. What is the average velocity in km/h?
2.explanation: Displacement = 0 (returns to start), so average velocity = 0, even though average speed = 6 km / 0.5 h = 12 km/h.

2.prompt: A train decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over a distance of 200 m. What is its acceleration in m/s²? (Give the magnitude.)
2.explanation: v² = u² + 2as → 10² = 30² + 2a(200) → 100 = 900 + 400a → a = −2 m/s². Magnitude 2 m/s² (deceleration).

2.prompt: A v–t graph shows an object moving at a constant 12 m/s for 8 s. What distance does it cover, in metres?
2.explanation: Area under the v–t line = 12 × 8 = 96 m. Area = distance.

3.prompt: A car covers the first half of a journey at 40 km/h and the second half (equal distance) at 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey, in km/h? (Give to one decimal place.)
3.explanation: For equal distances, average = 2·v1·v2/(v1+v2) = 2·40·60/100 = 48 km/h — the harmonic mean, NOT 50. Same total-over-total logic as the ratio topic.

3.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). How high does it rise, in metres?
3.explanation: At the top v = 0. v² = u² − 2gs → 0 = 20² − 2×10×s → s = 400/20 = 20 m. At the peak velocity is 0 but acceleration is still g.

3.prompt: A ball thrown straight up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²) — what is its total time in the air before returning to the throw height, in seconds?
3.explanation: Time up = u/g = 20/10 = 2 s; by symmetry time down = 2 s; total = 4 s. Use the up/down symmetry to halve the work.

3.prompt: A car moving at constant 50 km/h rounds a circular bend. During the turn, the car is:
choices: not accelerating, since speed is constant
accelerating, because the direction of velocity changes
at rest relative to the road
3.explanation: Velocity is a vector. Constant speed but changing direction means velocity changes, so there IS acceleration (centripetal — studied fully in Physics I1).

3.prompt: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration and travels a distance s in the first 4 s. How many times s does it travel in total after 8 s (i.e., find total distance ÷ s)?
3.explanation: s ∝ t² from rest (s = ½at²). Distance in 8 s vs 4 s scales as 8²/4² = 64/16 = 4. So total after 8 s is 4s. Recognising the t² proportionality is the shortcut.

physics.F2.electricity-i.subject: physics
physics.F2.electricity-i.title: Electricity I
physics.F2.electricity-i.summary: Current, voltage, resistance and Ohm's law, with series and parallel circuits.
physics.F2.electricity-i.notes:
# Electricity I

> [!intro] Current, voltage, resistance and Ohm's law, with series and parallel circuits.

## Ohm's law

Voltage drives current through resistance: V = IR. It is the central relationship of simple circuits and, like many physics laws, a proportionality.

## Series vs parallel

In series, current is the same and resistances add; in parallel, voltage is the same and currents split. These rules follow from conservation of charge and energy.

```formula Key formulas
V = IR (Ohm’s law)
Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …
Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
Series current is uniform; parallel voltage is uniform
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Two 4 Ω resistors in series across 8 V. Find the current.
> >
> > **Solution.** R = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. I = V/R = 8/8 = 1 A.

## What you should be able to do

- Define current, voltage, resistance
- Apply Ohm's law V = IR
- Analyse series and parallel circuits

---

physics.F2.heat-temperature.summary: The particle model of heat, temperature vs thermal energy, transfer methods and specific heat.
physics.F2.heat-temperature.notes:
# Heat & Temperature

> [!intro] The particle model of heat, temperature vs thermal energy, transfer methods and specific heat.

## Heat vs temperature

Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference. A spark is hot but carries little heat.

## Specific heat

Specific heat capacity is the energy to raise 1 kg by 1°C. Q = mcΔT lets you compute heating and cooling quantitatively.

```formula Key formulas
Q = mcΔT
Temperature ∝ average particle KE
Radiation needs no medium; convection needs a fluid
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Heat needed to raise 0.5 kg of water (c = 4200) by 20°C?
> >
> > **Solution.** Q = mcΔT = 0.5 × 4200 × 20 = 42000 J.

## What you should be able to do

- Distinguish heat from temperature
- Describe conduction, convection, radiation
- Use specific heat capacity

---

physics.F2.light-i.notes:
# Light I

> [!intro] Light as rays: reflection, refraction and simple lenses, using the geometry of similar triangles.

## Rays and reflection

Light travels in straight rays; on reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. This explains mirrors and shadows.

## Refraction and lenses

Light bends when it changes medium (refraction), which is how lenses form images. Ray diagrams predict image position, size and orientation.

```formula Key formulas
Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (from normal)
Refraction: light bends changing medium
Convex lens converges; concave diverges
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A ray hits a mirror 40° from the normal. Find the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
> >
> > **Solution.** Reflection angle = 40°. Angle between the two rays = 40° + 40° = 80°.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the laws of reflection and refraction
- Trace rays through mirrors and lenses
- Explain image formation

---

physics.F2.magnetism-i.notes:
# Magnetism I

> [!intro] Magnetic fields, electromagnets and the link between electricity and magnetism.

## Fields and poles

Magnets have north and south poles; like poles repel, unlike attract. Field lines run from north to south and show the field's direction and strength.

## Electromagnetism

A current creates a magnetic field around it. Coiling wire into a solenoid concentrates the field, making an electromagnet — the basis of motors and relays.

```formula Key formulas
Like poles repel, unlike attract
Field lines run N → S outside a magnet
A current creates a magnetic field (right-hand grip rule)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** How can you strengthen an electromagnet?
> >
> > **Solution.** Increase the current, add more coil turns, or insert a soft-iron core — each increases the magnetic field.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe magnetic fields and poles
- Explain electromagnets
- Relate current to magnetism

---

physics.F2.pressure-density.summary: Density as mass per volume, pressure in fluids, and buoyancy — more ratio reasoning applied.
physics.F2.pressure-density.notes:
# Pressure & Density

> [!intro] Density as mass per volume, pressure in fluids, and buoyancy — more ratio reasoning applied.

## Density and pressure are rates

Density = mass/volume and pressure = force/area — both are ratios. Pressure in a fluid increases with depth and acts equally in all directions.

## Buoyancy

A submerged object feels an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid it displaces (Archimedes). It floats when upthrust balances weight.

```formula Key formulas
Density ρ = m/V
Pressure P = F/A
Fluid pressure P = ρgh
Floats if ρ_object < ρ_fluid
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Find the pressure at the base of a 2 m column of water (ρ = 1000, g = 10).
> >
> > **Solution.** P = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 2 = 20000 Pa = 20 kPa.

## What you should be able to do

- Compute density and pressure
- Explain pressure in fluids
- Apply buoyancy and floating

---

physics.F2.sound-waves-i.notes:
# Sound & Waves I

> [!intro] Wave parameters, the wave equation v = fλ, and properties of sound.

## Wave anatomy

A wave has wavelength (length of one cycle), frequency (cycles per second) and amplitude (size). Speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by v = fλ — another rate relationship.

## Sound needs a medium

Sound is a pressure wave that needs particles to travel; it cannot cross a vacuum. Pitch relates to frequency, loudness to amplitude.

```formula Key formulas
v = fλ
Frequency ↔ pitch; amplitude ↔ loudness
Sound needs a medium (no vacuum)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A sound wave has frequency 340 Hz and wavelength 1 m. Find its speed.
> >
> > **Solution.** v = fλ = 340 × 1 = 340 m/s (the speed of sound in air).

## What you should be able to do

- Define frequency, wavelength, amplitude
- Use v = fλ
- Explain how sound travels

physics.I1.circular-motion-gravitation.summary: Centripetal acceleration, orbits and Newton's law of gravitation.
physics.I1.circular-motion-gravitation.notes:
# Circular Motion & Gravitation

> [!intro] Centripetal acceleration, orbits and Newton's law of gravitation.

## Centripetal force

Circular motion at constant speed still accelerates — toward the centre. A net centripetal force (mv²/r) is required; remove it and the object flies off tangentially.

## Gravitation

Every mass attracts every other with F = Gm₁m₂/r². This same force keeps planets in orbit, balancing the centripetal requirement.

```formula Key formulas
Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r (toward centre)
Centripetal force F = mv²/r
Gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r² (inverse-square)
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** If the distance between two masses triples, how does the gravitational force change?
> >
> > **Solution.** F ∝ 1/r². Tripling r gives F × 1/3² = 1/9 of the original force.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain centripetal force
- Use the gravitation law
- Describe orbital motion

---

physics.I1.energy-ii.notes:
# Energy II

> [!intro] Power, efficiency and energy resources, treated quantitatively.

## Power and efficiency

Power is the rate of doing work (P = W/t). Efficiency is useful output ÷ total input — always below 100% because some energy dissipates as heat.

## Energy in the real world

Every device transforms energy with losses. Comparing resources means comparing energy density, renewability and conversion efficiency.

```formula Key formulas
Power P = W/t = energy/time
Efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%
1 watt = 1 joule/second
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A motor does 600 J of useful work from 800 J input in 4 s. Find its power output and efficiency.
> >
> > **Solution.** Power (useful) = 600/4 = 150 W. Efficiency = 600/800 × 100 = 75%.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate power and efficiency
- Track energy through transformations
- Compare energy resources

---

physics.I1.kinematics-2d.notes:
# Kinematics in Two Dimensions

> [!intro] Vectors applied to motion — resolving into components and analysing projectiles.

## Independence of components

Horizontal and vertical motion are independent: gravity affects only the vertical. Splitting a velocity into x and y components (using trig) turns 2-D motion into two 1-D problems.

## Projectiles

A projectile has constant horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration g. Combining the two components gives its parabolic path, range and time of flight.

```formula Key formulas
vₓ = v cos θ, v_y = v sin θ
Horizontal: constant velocity; vertical: free fall (g)
Range depends on both components
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30°. Find its horizontal and vertical velocity components.
> >
> > **Solution.** vₓ = 20 cos30° = 20(0.866) ≈ 17.3 m/s. v_y = 20 sin30° = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s.

## What you should be able to do

- Resolve velocity into components
- Analyse projectile motion
- Treat horizontal and vertical motion independently

---

physics.I1.momentum-collisions.notes:
# Momentum & Collisions

> [!intro] Momentum, impulse and the conservation of momentum in collisions.

## Momentum and impulse

Momentum p = mv; impulse (force × time) changes momentum. A small force over a long time can produce the same change as a large brief force.

## Conservation in collisions

With no external force, total momentum is conserved in any collision. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic ones do not.

```formula Key formulas
Momentum p = mv
Impulse = FΔt = Δp
Conservation: total p before = total p after
Elastic conserves KE; inelastic does not
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits and sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley. Find their common speed.
> >
> > **Solution.** Conservation: 2×3 + 1×0 = (2+1)v → 6 = 3v → v = 2 m/s.

## What you should be able to do

- Compute momentum and impulse
- Apply conservation of momentum
- Distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions

physics.I1.newtons-laws-deepened.notes:
# Newton's Laws Deepened

> [!intro] Friction, inclined planes and connected systems of bodies.

## Friction

Friction opposes relative motion and is proportional to the normal force (F ≤ μN). It converts kinetic energy to heat and must be added to force diagrams.

## Inclines and systems

On a slope, resolve weight into components along and perpendicular to the surface. For connected bodies, apply F = ma to each and to the system.

```formula Key formulas
Friction f = μN
On an incline: along-slope mg sin θ, into-surface mg cos θ
Connected bodies share one acceleration
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A 10 kg block on a 30° frictionless incline. Find its acceleration (g = 10).
> >
> > **Solution.** a = g sin θ = 10 × sin30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s² down the slope.

## What you should be able to do

- Include friction in force analysis
- Solve inclined-plane problems
- Analyse connected bodies

---

physics.I2.electricity-ii.notes:
# Electricity II

> [!intro] EMF and internal resistance, Kirchhoff's laws, and capacitors (introductory).

## Real sources

A real cell has internal resistance, so its terminal voltage drops under load. EMF is the total energy per charge; some is lost inside the source.

## Kirchhoff's laws

Charge conservation gives the junction (current) law; energy conservation gives the loop (voltage) law. Together they solve any circuit.

```formula Key formulas
EMF ε = I(R + r), r = internal resistance
Kirchhoff current law: Σ currents in = Σ out
Kirchhoff voltage law: Σ voltages around a loop = 0
Capacitor: Q = CV
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A cell of EMF 6 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω drives 2 A. Find the terminal voltage.
> >
> > **Solution.** V = ε − Ir = 6 − 2(0.5) = 5 V.

## What you should be able to do

- Use EMF and internal resistance
- Apply Kirchhoff's laws
- Explain capacitor basics

---

physics.I2.kinematics-calculus.notes:
# Kinematics with Calculus

> [!intro] Position, velocity and acceleration as derivatives and integrals — co-taught with calculus.

## Motion is calculus

Velocity is the derivative of position; acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Integrating reverses this. This makes the "slope = rate, area = distance" idea exact.

## Non-uniform acceleration

When acceleration varies, the SUVAT equations fail but calculus still works — integrate the actual acceleration function to get velocity and position.

```formula Key formulas
v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt
x = ∫v dt, v = ∫a dt
Constant a → use SUVAT; varying a → integrate
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Position x = 3t² m. Find the velocity at t = 2 s.
> >
> > **Solution.** v = dx/dt = 6t. At t = 2: v = 12 m/s.

## What you should be able to do

- Relate position, velocity, acceleration by calculus
- Differentiate/integrate motion functions
- Handle non-uniform acceleration

---

physics.I2.oscillations-shm.notes:
# Oscillations (Simple Harmonic Motion)

> [!intro] Simple harmonic motion: restoring force, period, and energy exchange in oscillators.

## Restoring force

SHM happens when the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed back to equilibrium (F = −kx). Springs and small-angle pendulums are examples.

## Period and energy

The period depends on the system (mass and stiffness), not the amplitude. Energy sloshes between kinetic and potential twice per cycle.

```formula Key formulas
SHM: restoring force F = −kx
Period T = 1/f (independent of amplitude)
Max KE at equilibrium, max PE at extremes
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A mass on a spring completes 20 oscillations in 10 s. Find the period and frequency.
> >
> > **Solution.** T = 10/20 = 0.5 s. f = 1/T = 2 Hz.

## What you should be able to do

- Define SHM conditions
- Relate period to system parameters
- Describe energy in oscillation

---

physics.I2.thermal-physics.notes:
# Thermal Physics

> [!intro] The gas laws and kinetic theory — a topic shared with chemistry, taught once.

## Gas laws

Pressure, volume and temperature of a gas are linked: PV/T is constant, giving the ideal gas equation PV = nRT. Each individual law (Boyle, Charles) is a special case.

## Kinetic theory

A gas is countless particles in random motion; temperature measures their average kinetic energy. This microscopic picture explains the macroscopic gas laws.

```formula Key formulas
PV = nRT (T in kelvin)
Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
Charles: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
T(K) = T(°C) + 273
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** A gas at 1 atm and 300 K is heated to 600 K at constant volume. Find the new pressure.
> >
> > **Solution.** P/T constant: P₂ = P₁ × T₂/T₁ = 1 × 600/300 = 2 atm.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the gas laws
- Relate temperature to particle motion
- Use the ideal gas equation

---

physics.I2.waves-ii.summary: Superposition, standing waves, resonance and the Doppler effect.
physics.I2.waves-ii.notes:
# Waves II

> [!intro] Superposition, standing waves, resonance and the Doppler effect.

## Superposition

When waves overlap, displacements add. This produces interference — constructive (in phase) or destructive (out of phase) — and standing waves on strings and in pipes.

## Doppler effect

Relative motion between source and observer shifts the observed frequency: approaching raises pitch, receding lowers it. It applies to sound and light.

```formula Key formulas
Superposition: displacements add
Constructive: path difference = nλ; destructive = (n+½)λ
Doppler: approaching → higher observed frequency
```

> [!example] **Worked example**
> **Problem.** Two coherent waves meet with a path difference of one full wavelength. Constructive or destructive?
> >
> > **Solution.** Path difference = 1λ = a whole number of wavelengths → constructive interference (a bright/loud point).

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the principle of superposition
- Explain standing waves and resonance
- Describe the Doppler effect

---
